In separate co-refinement studies, task-matched estimators enable homogeneous composition across multiple neutron contrasts and heterogeneous multimodal composition of X-ray and neutron measurements. Together, these results establish compositional flow matching as a modular approach to uncertainty-aware inversion and co-refinement, with potential applicability to other scattering problems in which multiple observations constrain a common physical structure while retaining measurement-specific parameters.

papers.title: ABACUS: Program-Guided Multistep Reasoning over Frozen Judgment Models
papers.abstract: Judgment models answer semantic questions by scoring a finite set of candidate outcomes. Can reusable programs turn these local decisions into powerful multistep reasoning? We introduce \method, a framework that jointly constructs judgment schemas and composition programs for frozen judgment models. A generative teacher designs the procedure offline; the judgment model resolves local semantic questions online, and the saved program composes its decisions into an answer. We study three allocations of design effort between humans and the teacher, focusing on construction through a shared interface. We instantiate the framework with Kev. On three selected BIG-Bench Hard tasks, nine independently constructed programs solve all 450 executions of 150 development inputs. A separate deployment study freezes three programs after development-set reference-agreement refinement and evaluates them on 600 held-out questions. These programs achieve near-perfect 99.67\% macro accuracy, versus 64.00\% for direct Kev and 68.80\% for final-answer-only Qwen3.5-4B. They attain comparable observed accuracy to Qwen's unrestricted response policy (99.07\%) with an \textbf{8.43-fold online speedup}: 0.255 versus 2.150 seconds per question. These results show how reusable programs can substantially expand the reasoning capability of a compact judgment model while keeping its parameters fixed.

papers.title: Random Clocks on Computation Paths: How Far Can They Reach, and When Does Stepping Back Help?
papers.abstract: A lookup, a prediction, or a return to a saved state can bring us to a stage of a computation without replaying the intervening steps. We model this access by a random clock, fixed in advance, that moves along a deterministic computation by jumping forward or stepping backward. Each observation costs one unit. We ask which language classes can be recognized with polynomially many observations. For clocks with independent jumps, the resulting class depends primarily on the tail of the forward-jump distribution. We give explicit clocks that recognize exactly $\mathrm{EXP}$, $\mathrm{2EXP}$, and each quasipolynomial class $\mathrm{QP}_k$, with the latter forming a strict hierarchy between $\mathrm{P}$ and $\mathrm{EXP}$. A backward-drifting clock with sufficiently rare long forward jumps recognizes exactly the reverse-definite languages, whose membership is determined by a bounded prefix of the input. Between the reverse-definite languages and $\mathrm{P}$, we construct infinitely many pairwise incomparable classes. Finally, we construct families in which every forward-only clock recognizes only languages in $\mathrm{P}$, while allowing occasional one-step backward moves yields $\mathrm{EXP}$ and larger classes.

papers.title: The 3-adic Steinberg block and a categorical 3-adic local Langlands correspondence for $\text{GL}_2(\mathbb{Q}_3)$
papers.abstract: We extend the work of Johansson-Newton-Wang-Erickson on a categorical $p$-adic Langlands correspondence over $\text{GL}_2(\mathbb{Q}_p)$ to $p = 3$ by recontextualizing their construction in the Steinberg case. We produce a novel, more categorical method of analyzing the properties of this construction without requiring an explicit algebraic presentation. As input to this argument, we also perform some new analysis of the representation theory of the $3$-adic Steinberg block of $\text{GL}_2(\mathbb{Q}_3)$, obtaining results complementing those of Paškūnas.

papers.title: A Conditional No-Hair Theorem for Transformers: How Language Models Forget Their Prompt
papers.abstract: A black hole retains only a few conserved charges of the matter it formed from. We are inspired to make the analogy and we ask how much an autoregressive transformer retains of its prompt after generating $t$ tokens. For two prompts followed by the same continuation, the difference of their hidden states decays approximately as a power law $t^{-α}$, where $α=1$ is the rate at which a fixed prompt's share of uniform attention shrinks. Beyond the first layers, trained models forget faster ($α\approx0.55$--$0.7$) than untrained ones of the same architecture ($α\approx0.2$--$0.5$). For finite-depth pre-LN softmax transformers with bounded attention logits and non-degenerate pre-norm activations, we prove that this offset is $O\big(P(\log t)^{L-1}/t\big)$ for prompt length $P$ and depth $L$: the prompt's direct influence is diluted as the context grows, and \emph{relay} through continuation tokens adds only logarithmic factors. Conditional on the generated text, the prompt's influence on the next token thus vanishes. The bound fixes only the asymptotic shape and is uninformative at the lengths we measure in trained networks; an exactly solvable linear relay model shows that it cannot be improved and accounts for the untrained curves. Cancelling the dilution with a logit bias on the prompt stops the decay early in training, and training suppresses relay by about one billion tokens, before attention sinks form. A toolkit that measures $α$ for any Hugging Face causal language model is publicly available.

papers.title: Dynamical Kernel Attention: Estimating the Present from a Record of the Past
papers.abstract: Self-attention encodes where a past token lies, but not how its uncertainty grows with time: evidence accumulates without bound as the context grows, and nothing indicates which tokens are safe to discard. We introduce Dynamical Kernel Attention (DKA), which derives attention from robust estimation of a latent state governed by a stochastic differential equation. Under this model, each head draws bounded evidence from any context. This lets each head abstain when relevant evidence is weak, and gives each head a memory window outside which discarding tokens changes its output by a provably bounded amount. On language modeling, DKA outperforms RoPE within the training length and ALiBi far beyond it, and matches sliding-window attention with a substantially smaller key-value cache.

papers.title: Canonical Layer Inference for Deep Gaussian Processes via Symmetry-Breaking Augmentation
papers.abstract: Deep Gaussian processes (DGPs) are flexible priors for estimating compositional functions, but function-level accuracy does not determine their intermediate-layer representations. The basic obstruction is an adjacent-layer symmetry: applying an invertible transformation and its inverse to two adjacent layers leaves the composed regression map unchanged. Under explicit symmetry and prior-comparability conditions, we show that the posterior may not concentrate on any prescribed intermediate-layer representation, even when the composed regression function is estimable. We introduce a layerwise exponential tilt of the DGP prior, using a penalty proportional to each hidden layer's distance from the identity map, with stronger weights on earlier layers. The methodology links an exact posterior-odds rule along likelihood-preserving symmetries to quantitative control of redundant layers. Under proxy and local prior-mass conditions, we derive a penalty window that preserves function-level fractional posterior contraction while localizing redundant layers at certain radius. The resulting design rule calibrates representation regularization to the function-estimation rate. It favors decompositions with earlier layers close to identity; uniqueness and automatic depth selection are not established. The general theory and methodology are supported with detailed examples.

papers.title: Agentic In-Context Learning: What Algorithms Can Transformers Learn in Closed-Loop Interaction?
papers.abstract: The learning algorithm view of in-context learning (ICL) studies how fixed-parameter Transformers learn from supplied examples. Language model agents extend this setting through interaction: their actions determine what evidence enters context next. We call this regime Agentic In-Context Learning (Agentic ICL). Existing studies largely depend on externally supplied contexts or reward-bearing interaction histories, while work on general tool-using agents lacks a learning algorithm view. We represent an interactive learner by its state, update, and decision rule, covering active learning, bandits, and online reinforcement learning (RL). For expressivity, we construct causal Transformers that approximate these algorithms over a finite horizon, and bound the resulting loss in return. For training, we characterize when optimizing process rewards preserves behavior that maximizes the final outcome. Distillation experiments show that Transformers can learn to execute three representative recursions. We then train models from outcome or process rewards without oracle action or state targets, as in RL post-training. Different rewards yield distinct decision policies. Improving the alignment of process supervision with outcome-optimal action preferences shifts learned decisions accordingly. Such behavioral differences persist in a pretrained language model across textual paraphrases.

papers.title: Does On-Policy Distillation Need to Complete Every Rollout?
papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) transfers teacher knowledge to a student through feedback on student-generated rollouts, but generating complete rollouts and computing per-token teacher feedback are computationally expensive. Existing truncation methods save computation by stopping rollouts early. However, they do not compensate for truncated token gradients, which biases the gradient estimates and changes Vanilla OPD's original training objective. Furthermore, their truncation decisions rely on assumptions about supervision quality or criteria that may not generalize across settings. We introduce Stochastic Truncated On-Policy Distillation (STOPD), which accelerates OPD by randomly truncating student rollouts and correcting the resulting sampling bias with blockwise inverse-probability weighting (IPW). At each training step, we sample a stopping position for each rollout before generation and let the student generate until that position or natural termination. We obtain teacher feedback on every generated token and use blockwise IPW to compensate for the lower probability of retaining later tokens while controlling the weights. We prove that this weighting preserves Vanilla OPD's gradient sum in expectation and derive one-step update-error bounds for SGD, Adam, and Muon. We evaluate STOPD across multiple teacher-student model pairs, task domains, and optimizers. STOPD reduces generated tokens by 25-48% while maintaining accuracy comparable to Vanilla OPD, achieving 1.3-2.2x training speedups.

papers.title: Infinite Derivatives and Local Extrema of the Delange Function of Every Base
papers.abstract: For an integer $q\ge2$, the Delange function of base $q$ is $T_q(x)=\sum_{j=0}^\infty q^{-j}τ_q(q^jx)$, where $τ_q$ has period $1$, is linear on $[k/q,(k+1)/q]$ for integers $0\le k<q$, and satisfies $τ_q(k/q)=k(q-k)/q$ for $0\le k\le q$. Thus $T_2$ is Takagi's function. In the Hamming graph on $\{0,1,\ldots,q-1\}^n$, two words are adjacent exactly when they differ in one letter. For integers $n\ge1$ and $0\le m\le q^n$, $q^nT_q(m/q^n)$ is the smallest number of edges leaving a set of $m$ vertices, which is known. We characterize infinite derivatives by the base $q$ digits $ξ_1,ξ_2,\ldots$ of $x\in[0,1)$. Outside the $q$-adic rationals $m/q^n$ with integers $m$ and $n\ge0$, the right derivative is $+\infty$ exactly when $\sum_{j=1}^n(q-1-2ξ_j)\to+\infty$. The condition for the left derivative to be $+\infty$ also involves the lengths of the maximal strings of zeros. For $-\infty$, the sides and the digits $0$ and $q-1$ are exchanged. The local minima are exactly the $q$-adic rationals. The local maxima are exactly the points $(m+u)/q^n+k$ with integers $k$, $m$, $n$ such that $n\ge0$, $0\le m<q^n$, and the base $q$ digit sum of $m$ is $(q-1)n/2$, where $u$ maximizes $T_q$ on $[0,1]$. For odd $q$, we have $u=1/2$ and every local maximum is strict. For even $q$, there are uncountably many such $u$ and no local maximum is strict. We also find the maximum on each interval $[m/q^n,(m+1)/q^n]$ and all points attaining it. For an integer $h$ with $1\le h\le q^n/2$, we determine the minimum number of edges whose deletion disconnects the graph into components with at least $h$ vertices, including a digit criterion for equality with the minimum boundary at size $h$. Almost every level set $\{x\in[0,1]:T_q(x)=y\}$ is finite, whereas the level set through almost every point is uncountable. Here almost every refers to Lebesgue measure.

papers.title: Let the Mind Conceive, Let the Hand Achieve: Coupling Grounded Action and Progress Evaluation for Long-Horizon Manipulation
papers.abstract: A robot following a multi-step instruction needs to act on the right objects in the right order, even as the scene changes. It must also maintain awareness of task progress and determine when to advance. To address these challenges, we introduce Orchestra, an agent harness that separates task planning and execution management from action generation. Orchestra decomposes a complete multimodal instruction into ordered subtasks, tracks completed steps, and updates the locations of relevant objects and destinations during execution. It maintains a shared context containing the active subtask, spatial grounding, and recent observations. An action policy uses this context to generate actions, while a separately trained progress evaluator estimates when to advance to the next subtask. To evaluate whether robots trained on atomic instructions and short trajectories can execute longer subtask sequences, we introduce a benchmark named RMBench-Compose. Orchestra achieves a mean success rate of $68.22\%$ across nine RMBench tasks, outperforming Mem-0 by $26.22$ percentage points. On RMBench-Compose, it achieves an Average Success Length (ASL) of $7.35$ subtasks, $2.46$ times that of HarnessVLA. Across four real-world multi-step tasks, it improves mean ASL by $25.0\%$ over Orchestra using the base $π_{0.5}$ policy. These results show that Orchestra helps robots carry out longer sequences of subtasks while preserving the requested subtask order and acting on the specified objects. Our code and project page are available at https://youpengwen.github.io/Orchestra

papers.title: PHastR: Faster Minimal Perfect Hashing with Rotated Layouts
papers.abstract: We present PHastR, a minimal perfect hash function of the PHast family. Like PHast+, the fast-to-build variant of PHast, PHastR finds feasible seeds with bit-parallel operations: its seeds move keys along rings of slots, and to evaluate the seeds of a bucket it cyclically shifts, for each key, a word recording which slots of its ring are used. Unlike PHast+, however, it is almost immune to self-collisions, which make two keys of a bucket collide for (almost) all its seeds: more than a third of the buckets bumped by PHast+ with wrapping and multiplier 3 contain one. With 8-bit seeds, PHastR uses $1.94$ bits per key, essentially the same space as the best variant of PHast+ with wrapping, but it is built in $37\%$ of the time, and its queries are $34\%$ faster on $10^9$ keys, as it bumps $0.5\%$ of the keys instead of $3.9\%$; they are faster also than those of PHast, which takes almost thirteen times as long to build, and than those of PtrHash, which uses more than one bit per key more. With a larger expected bucket size PHastR comes within $0.02$ bits per key of the space of PHast, using $1.90$ bits per key, and its queries are still about as fast. Its construction also scales better with the number of threads: with all the threads of a 96-core machine it is more than two and a half times faster than that of PHast+. An offline construction built PHastR on a trillion keys in $9.3$ hours on a single machine. Finally, we argue that when each key can be placed only within a range of $W$ slots, every placement of $n$ random keys on $n$ slots, however found, must bump on large key sets a constant fraction of the keys: we derive an asymptotic lower bound of about $0.1/W$ on the expected value of this fraction, and we prove that, in a Poisson model, the best placement bumps about $1/2W$ of the keys, which is about one tenth of the keys bumped by PHastR.

papers.title: SarcasTraps: Effect of Sarcasm on Turkish Hate Speech Detection
papers.abstract: Standard hate speech detection datasets often emphasize explicit harmful language, but directed harm can also be expressed indirectly, without clearly hateful wording. Sarcasm is one such form of indirect expression, as it can convey harmful intent through mock praise, exaggeration, humor, or apparent politeness. In this paper, we introduce SarcasTraps, a targeted external test set for analyzing the effect of sarcasm on Turkish hate speech detection. SarcasTraps contains 479 entries annotated along two dimensions: hate speech and sarcasm. We train classifiers using BERTurk and XLM-RoBERTa on two existing Turkish hate speech datasets and evaluate them on SarcasTraps, using it strictly as an external test set. We also evaluate GPT-4.1 and Llama-3.3-70B in a zero-shot setting on SarcasTraps. Results show that sarcasm substantially affects hate speech detection. Fine-tuned encoder models lose recall on sarcastic hate, while zero-shot LLMs maintain higher recall but suffer substantial precision drops on sarcastic examples. These findings show that both fine-tuned hate speech detectors and zero-shot LLMs struggle when sarcasm is involved, and SarcasTraps provides quantitative evidence of this challenge through a targeted Turkish test set. Due to the presence of sensitive and hateful language, SarcasTraps will be shared upon request for academic research purposes. Warning: This paper has examples from the dataset which contains offensive and hateful content towards groups of people.

papers.title: ANCHOR: Assessing Naturalistic Constraint Hierarchies and Ordering in Repository-Grounded Agentic Coding
papers.abstract: For repository-grounded coding agents, a functionally correct patch is not necessarily an acceptable one: developers also constrain how the task must be carried out-modification scope, workflow order, validation, tool use, and reporting. This capability, which we call engineering constraint following, remains largely invisible to current evaluations. We introduce ANCHOR (Assessing Naturalistic Constraint Hierarchies and Ordering in Repository-Grounded Agentic Coding), a benchmark built on naturalistic, multilingual repository tasks spanning eight language groups. ANCHOR combines (i) a hierarchical taxonomy of 10 categories and 78 leaf types distilled from real developer interactions, (ii) an automated pipeline that instantiates task-grounded atomic constraints and composes them into typed AND/THEN/PRIORITY relations, and (iii) a trajectory-grounded evaluation framework that checks both the code diff and the execution trajectory with rule-based and LLM judges. Across 19 agent configurations spanning 2 scaffolds and 10 foundation models on 358 tasks, the strongest measured system, Claude Opus 4.8 under Cline, reaches 70.1% atomic compliance and 63.7% relation compliance, while 19.0% of tasks pass every scored checklist item under the strict all-item FCCR criterion. A five-engineer audit of constraints from 50 instances reports 94% feasibility, 94% repository consistency, and 96% realism. In the primary paired set (14 configurations), the mean signed change in task completion after adding constraints is +0.7 percentage points; individual changes vary in both directions. These results distinguish functional success from constraint compliance, with failures concentrated in workflow ordering, tool-use discipline, and reporting, and substantial interactions between models and scaffolds.

papers.title: Communication, Vocalisation, and Language
papers.abstract: The contention is that the current batch of Large Language Models don't *understand* language, but they *do* it. Rather than LLMs forming some kind of ``distributed representation'' of symbols, the claim is that LLMs are capturing ``Cultural Intelligence'' and grounding symbols in what the sociologists call practices.

papers.title: Stereo-Planner: Learning Stereo-to-Trajectory Planning for Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Quadrotor Navigation
papers.abstract: Existing navigation systems commonly rely on dedicated depth sensors or explicit depth reconstruction, while learning to generate trajectories directly from RGB images remains challenging due to the sim-to-real domain gap. In this work, we propose Stereo-Planner, an end-to-end vision-to-trajectory framework that enables zero-shot sim-to-real planning from stereo RGB observations. The key idea is to formulate trajectory generation as state- and scale-conditioned querying of latent stereo geometry. A Scene Representor incorporates a pretrained vision grounding foundation model to extract geometric cues shared across simulated and real-world environments, supporting generalization across visual domains. A lightweight Trajectory Decoder then translates these representations into trajectories through interleaved attention, separating trajectory-state interaction from scene-feature retrieval and incorporating the stereo baseline as a metric-scale cue. With these designs, Stereo-Planner is trained entirely on simulated data by minimizing differentiable trajectory costs and deployed directly in real-world environments without fine-tuning. Benchmark results demonstrate strong cross-scene generalization, with a 95% success rate in simulation environments at a commanded speed of 8 m/s, and competitive performance against depth-based planners using only stereo RGB observations for scene perception. Furthermore, deployment on a compact quadrotor equipped with an NVIDIA Orin NX enables autonomous flight at speeds of approaching 8 m/s, with a mean onboard vision-to-action inference time of 14.44 ms. The software, simulation environments, and hardware designs will be open-sourced at https://github.com/Stereo-Planner/Stereo-Planner.

papers.title: Retrieving Complementary Evidence for Multi-Hop RAG with Semantic Gain Graphs
papers.abstract: Multi-hop retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) requires finding documents whose evidence is useful in combination. Query relevance and graph connectivity help locate related content, but neither directly measures the additional information one document contributes given another. We introduce SG$^2$RAG, a framework that represents this complementarity through semantic gain. Offline, a large language model assesses the relevant and nonredundant information contributed by one chunk given another within neighborhoods proposed by semantic similarity. These ordered assessments are aggregated into symmetric edge weights to construct a reusable Semantic Gain Graph. Online, controlled Personalized PageRank starts from query-relevant seeds and ranks complementary evidence beyond the initial retrieval set. Experiments on MuSiQue, 2Wiki, and HotpotQA with two language model backbones show that SG$^2$RAG achieves the best average EM, F1, and Recall@10 among the evaluated single-retrieval methods. Under identical candidate support and propagation, semantic gain improves average F1 and Recall@10 over similarity weighting by 4.08 and 4.31 points. Analyses of supporting documents and improvements in three iterative retrieval frameworks further support its effectiveness as a reusable retrieval component.

papers.title: Natural Code Transformation Confuses Agents in Vulnerability Analysis
papers.abstract: Having demonstrated a strong potential for automating vulnerability discovery, AI agents can also be used to attack software systems at scale. Today's software systems need mechanisms to level the playing field by slowing down potential attacks, giving them time to patch vulnerabilities and strengthen software. Along this line, our study of agent trajectories in vulnerability analysis shows a surprising finding: agents produce dramatically different results across real-world code commits that carry the same functionality and the same vulnerability. This phenomenon appears consistently in multiple code domains and vulnerability categories. It motivates us to study natural and functionality-preserving code transformations derived from real-world software development, and their potential as a defense against attacker agents. We build a corpus of natural transformations by mining recurring development patterns from real-world code commits, and apply them to evaluate impact on agentic vulnerability analysis. Our results show that even a single form of transformation can effectively "confuse" frontier agents, e.g., Claude Mythos 5.2 with Claude Code, reducing successes in vulnerability discovery. We also study different agent failures, whether transformations can be composed to provide stronger protection, and adaptive attackers who seek to reverse them. Overall, our study of natural code transformation significantly expands the research space of using code transformations to defend against malicious agents.

papers.title: ECGGuard: Deep Watermarking of Electrocardiogram Signals With Error-Correcting Codes
papers.abstract: Wearable electrocardiogram (ECG) recordings pass through multiple networks and systems before automated interpretation, leaving patient metadata vulnerable to loss. Digital watermarking can embed this metadata in the signal, but conventional methods fail under time shifts, and high waveform similarity does not guarantee the same downstream diagnosis. We present \rev{ECGGuard}, a deep watermarking framework for single-lead ECG. A fully convolutional generator embeds the payload without signal quantization, a detector decodes the message frame by frame and checks for watermark presence, and during training a frozen arrhythmia classifier penalizes changes that would alter its predictions. Because high bit accuracy does not ensure whole-message recovery, the payload is protected by extended Hamming codes, \rev{a validation-selected channel ordering}, and soft-decision decoding. On the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database, \rev{averaged over three training runs, ECGGuard} keeps bit accuracy above \rev{98\%} under time shifts of 10 to 50 samples, where transform-domain baselines drop to chance. The coded 16-bit payload is recovered exactly in \rev{99.95\%} of clean segments\rev{, in over 96\%} under time shifts, 10\% sample deletion, or 10\% packet loss\rev{, and in 99.1\% for unseen subjects}. \rev{For the guiding classifier, the diagnostic loss limits the drop in ventricular-beat sensitivity to 1.6 percentage points on the test records (35.0 without it) and to 12.2 points for unseen subjects (67.0 without it); the drop grows to 10.3 points for independently trained classifiers, and the protection does not transfer to an external database.} \rev{ECGGuard} has 0.56 million parameters and needs about \rev{19}~ms per segment on a desktop CPU.

papers.title: Reassessing the $X(2370)$ in $J/ψ\toγK_S^0K_S^0π^0$ beyond the one-dimensional mass projections
papers.abstract: The BESIII Collaboration recently extracted the properties of the $X(2370)$ from a fit to the one-dimensional $K_S^0K_S^0π^0$ invariant-mass spectrum in $J/ψ\toγK_S^0K_S^0π^0$. The intermediate two-body structures visible in the mass correlations, including the $K_0^*(1430)$ bands, require a coherent treatment of cross-channel interference when interpreting the enhancement near 2.3 GeV. We reassess the need for an additional $X(2370)$ contribution by fitting the published data using an effective coupled-channel framework with an approximate detection efficiency depending on the three-body invariant mass. The three-body parent amplitude is parameterized using a $K$-matrix that describes scattering among several quasi-two-body channels. The seven- and eight-bare-state models give similar mass distributions. Adding the eighth bare state lowers the Poisson deviance by 1.22% and produces an additional pole at $E=(2419-i152)$ MeV, substantially broader than the $X(2370)$ mass-width reference. This pole is model-dependent, and its identification with the $X(2370)$ is not clear. The present analysis does not establish the need for an additional $X(2370)$ contribution in $J/ψ\toγK_S^0K_S^0π^0$, thereby weakening the flavor-singlet argument based on the suppression of $K^*\bar K$ relative to the total $K\bar Kπ$ contribution. A more comprehensive experimental amplitude analysis, incorporating coherent interference, mass and angular correlations, and detector effects across related decay channels, is needed to establish the role and decay properties of the $X(2370)$.

papers.title: Extremal black hole mimickers: geometry, stability, and long-delay signal trains
papers.abstract: We present a spacetime that serves as a horizonless mimicker of extremal black holes. Unlike previously studied mimickers of black holes with non-degenerate horizons, whose geometries are of the wormhole type and consist of two asymptotically flat regions connected by a very long throat, the mimicker of an extremal black hole possesses a single asymptotically flat region at one end and an infinitely long throat at the other. In the throat region, the spacetime approaches the direct-product geometry $M_{1,1} \times S^2$, where $M_{1,1}$ is two-dimensional Minkowski spacetime and $S^2$ is the two-sphere. We investigate scalar-field dynamics and the fate of the Aretakis instability. Although Aretakis-like modes arise in a local analysis of the throat, they do not lead to a physical instability of the mimicker. A scalar perturbation initially localized in the throat gives rise, at late times, to a sequence of signals with a characteristic separation $t_{\rm delay}\sim 1/λ$, where $λ\ll 1$ is a deformation parameter. This timescale is parametrically larger than the echo time $t_{\rm echo}\sim \ln(1/λ)$ characteristic of non-extremal black-hole mimickers. We refer to this sequence as a {\it long-delay signal train}. Geometrically, the periodicity of the long-delay signals is associated with periodic geodesics on $S^2$. We then extend the construction to extremal Kerr. In this case, the throat region approaches a generalized product geometry involving $M_{1,1}$ and a two-dimensional surface $Σ_2$. The corresponding signals are expected to form a quasi-periodic signal train, reflecting the quasi-periodic geodesic motion on $Σ_2$. We also comment on the generalization to wormhole mimickers of non-extremal black holes and on the implications of these results for unitarity in the context of the AdS/CFT correspondence.

papers.title: Relocating Nonlinearity: How a Downstream Learner Reshapes What Genetic Programming Must Evolve
papers.abstract: Genetic programming was conceived as a way of evolving solutions: the program is the answer, and fitness is the error of its own output. A substantial line of work instead makes the program an input to a separate learner, so fitness measures the learner's output. Which learner to attach matters and depends on the problem, with no account of what decides it. What makes a target hard for genetic programming is how much nonlinearity the program must build by composing primitives; any nonlinearity the learner supplies, the program is spared. Here we show that how much the program must still build is decided by which learner is attached, and is measurable on the programs themselves. In Boolean domains, where a target's nonlinearity is exactly its Fourier degree, we tune that degree from one to six with everything else fixed. Conditioned on success, a linear learner forces the evolved program to the target's degree exactly, at one through six without exception over thirty runs per setting, while tree ensembles succeed with far simpler programs and four times as often. Where the target's structure is known, the learner can be chosen from that structure rather than from the target's reputation for difficulty: our control target has lower degree than the parity problems yet gains nothing from a nonlinear learner. Where it is not, the same quantities serve as diagnostics: the degree of the evolved program is free to compute during any run and shows whether the learner is contributing nothing or carrying the model; on two measured datasets the resulting procedure picks the right learner before any evolution is run. A warning follows: evolution internalises what the learner supplies in only four of sixty-three conditions and grows more dependent on it in forty-four. The more capable the learner, the less of the model is left legible in the program.

papers.title: Spectral Recovery of Point Clouds from Noisy Geometric Graphs
papers.abstract: We study the problem of recovering low-dimensional latent geometry from a random geometric graph generated by noisy, high-dimensional data. Specifically, we analyze the performance of a spectral embedding algorithm on the Signal+Noise Graph Model, in which vertices are associated to points perturbed by Gaussian noise, and edges are included for pairs whose inner product exceeds a specified alignment threshold. In the high-dimensional regime where the number $n$ of points and the ambient dimension $d$ both tend to infinity, we show that under a spectral gap condition, the top eigenvectors and eigenvalues of the graph's adjacency matrix can be used to approximately recover the point cloud up to an orthogonal transformation. We illustrate our results on point clouds sampled from nested spheres and high-dimensional sinusoid curves.

papers.title: No Need to Stop the Fleet: Localized Anomaly Isolation via Dead Zones in AGV Fleets
papers.abstract: Automated Guided Vehicle (AGV) fleets in production and logistics environments rely on a system-wide emergency stop to handle local anomalies such as malfunctions, hazards, or contaminated areas. While safe, this approach halts the entire fleet even when only a small area is affected, causing unnecessary downtime. This paper proposes dead zones -- a formally defined localized isolation approach that serves as an additional fail-operational mechanism for situations where a full system-wide halt is not strictly needed. Rather than shutting down the entire fleet, a dead zone isolates the anomalous area, allowing unaffected robots to continue operating normally. We introduce two operational strategies: basic dead zone handling, in which affected robots enter a dead zone and stop, and dead zone handling with escaping, in which robots that are sufficiently far from a dead zone reroute around it. For escaping on counterclockwise trajectories we prove collision-freedom with a bounded arrival delay for all escaping robots, provided a minimum pairwise separation is kept between robots. Experimental evaluation confirms the theoretical guarantees and characterizes the throughput tradeoffs between all three approaches: full emergency stop, basic dead zone handling, and dead zone handling with escaping.

papers.title: Can Power Draw Constrain Covert Compute? Limits of Analogue Verification for AI Governance
papers.abstract: Frontier AI treaties or agreements on limiting computation require external verification; an external auditor must be able to confirm how much computation actually ran and that parties are adhering to the agreement. Analogue, off-chip measurements such as power draw provide an information channel for verification. It is unknown how well these analogue channels can constrain the amount of computation against an adversary who actively tries to subvert the audit. We derive a closed form for $β$, the largest hidden computation a power trace cannot exclude, as a fraction of the declared machine capacity. Measurements on NVIDIA A100 GPUs give $β= 1.16$ in the worst case, while an adversarial matched-energy schedule hides at least $0.41$. Analogue power measurements alone therefore constrain compute weakly. Additional restrictions granted by the threat model, such as the ability of the verifier to re-execute the declared work at an observed operating point, let the verifier push $β$ down to $0.059$ in the maximally restricted case. This gives a quantitative estimate of what analogue measurements can contribute to compute verification.

papers.title: AEGIS: Differentiable Mars Climate Model with Neural Closures
papers.abstract: General circulation models (GCMs) are the primary tool for simulating planetary atmospheres. They play a vital role in understanding Mars's atmosphere, as forecasting its unique weather is mission-critical for operations such as entry, descent, and landing. Mars poses unusual challenges for these models, as observations are sparse compared to Earth. In addition, a thin $CO_2$ atmosphere alongside a radiatively active dust cycle creates a volatile atmosphere with large diurnal temperature swings and no true terrestrial analog for validation. Existing Mars GCMs, including the LMD PCM, the NASA Ames Mars GCM, and PlanetWRF, are mature and physically detailed but are implemented in legacy Fortran with finite-difference or finite-volume solvers, and they do not expose gradients for calibration or machine learning. Here we present AEGIS, a modular differentiable Mars climate model that couples Mars's unique atmospheric physics to the Dinosaur dynamical core, with interfaces for neural closures. We showcase stable ten-Mars-year simulations that reproduce the seasonal $CO_2$ cycle while conserving the total $CO_2$ inventory, capture realistic large-scale surface-temperature structure, and produce surface pressure that follows Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA) topography. Gradients through coupled trajectories agree with finite differences and support physical calibration and neural training. We compare with conventional GCMs, highlighting the framework's computational efficiency and differentiability.

papers.title: A Dubnov-Ivanov-Nagata-Higman Theorem for NIP nilrings
papers.abstract: We prove that NIP nilrings of bounded nilexponent are nilpotent. We also deduce that NIP $ω$-categorical $n$-Engel Lie algebras of characteristic $p>n$ are nilpotent, yielding a case of the Lie algebra analogous of Wilson conjecture for $ω$-categorical groups.

papers.title: AVL-JEPA: Preventing Causal Dynamics Information Collapse In Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture World Models
papers.abstract: Joint embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) predict future latent representations without reconstructing observations, enabling world models to focus on high-level semantic dynamics. However, a JEPA can preserve high dimensional visual information while discarding information about the physical consequences of actions. We call this failure mode causal dynamics information collapse and propose action-grounded vision-invariance latent (AVL) to prevent this collapse. We first use the executed action as an auxiliary dynamics anchor that encourages the model to preserve dynamics information, and then use a vision-invariance pathway which aligns perturbed and clean latent predictions without discarding dynamics information, forcing the model to fully understand and utilize causal dynamics information. We validate AVL on four robotic control tasks (TwoRoom, PushT, OGBench Cube, and Reacher), showing that it substantially improves success rates under visual perturbations while preserving clean-environment performance. We further evaluate physical consequence alignment, clean-noisy dynamics consistency, and the causal effect of targeted transition subspace erasure. Collectively, these results indicate that dynamic information causally relevant to planning is preserved from collapse under AVL.

papers.title: Reliable Self-Evolution with Imperfect Proxy Rewards
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based self-evolving search is a promising approach to scientific discovery. However, high-fidelity evaluation of every candidate is prohibitively expensive in some domains. Self-evolving systems in such settings therefore rely on low-cost but imperfect proxy rewards, which may assign high scores to infeasible candidates. These false positives may contaminate both the final output and the feedback used to guide subsequent generations. This motivates statistically calibrated reward intervals for more reliable self-evolving search. We propose Conformal Interval-Driven Self-Evolution (CISE), which constructs candidate-specific reward intervals using conditional conformal inference and iteration-wise online density-ratio estimation. CISE uses conservative interval-based rewards for evolutionary feedback and returns candidates only when all required property intervals lie entirely within their respective feasible regions. We derive fixed-iteration coverage results under explicit assumptions of independence and covariate shift. We evaluate CISE on three self-evolving search tasks in materials science. In our experiments, all candidates returned by CISE are true positives under high-fidelity evaluation, whereas the baselines return more candidates but include false positives. These results highlight the value of a smaller, more precise shortlist when downstream validation budgets are limited. Our repository is available at https://github.com/MLAI-Yonsei/CISE.git.

papers.title: Transient resonances of chaotic orbits in magnetized black hole spacetimes: an event-based frequency-ratio diagnostic
papers.abstract: The geodesic equations of the Kerr spacetime are separable, and this separability is what makes orbital dynamics around black holes tractable. An external electromagnetic field removes it, the motion turns chaotic, and the orbit wanders between resonances for irregular and unequal intervals; a long-time Poincaré section returns a single static blur, so that it records where an orbit has been but not when. We introduce the sliding-window frequency ratio, an event-based diagnostic that counts polar turning events within a window of fixed radial-cycle number and returns the local ratio of the two frequencies without any spectral decomposition; for regular motion with bounded count deviations, the error falls off as the window widens. We first establish that a single globally chaotic orbit in a magnetized black hole spacetime pays temporally ordered visits to distinct resonances, and that the corresponding section structure appears only in those intervals that the event counts select. A charged orbit in magnetized Kerr spacetime dwells near 3/5 and later near 4/7, opening fivefold and sevenfold structures, while a photon in Schwarzschild--Melvin spacetime holds 4/5 across a fivefold pattern. Because we keep every event time, we can replot each selected interval as its own section, and integer counts then agree with phase-space geometry. These visits control the phase accumulated along an orbit, and they therefore bear on any orbit-based probe of strong-field black hole geometry.

papers.title: Determining $W^{1,n}$ conductivities for Calderón's problem in $\mathbb{R}^n$
papers.abstract: We establish a global uniqueness result at the critical Sobolev regularity for the isotropic Calderón problem in all dimensions $n \ge 4$. More precisely, for every $n \ge 4$ and every bounded Lipschitz domain $Ω\subset \mathbb{R}^n$, any real-valued, uniformly elliptic scalar conductivity $γ\in W^{1,n}(Ω)$ is uniquely determined by its full Dirichlet-to-Neumann map. Together with the known results for $n=2,3,4$ in the literature, this settles a long-standing open problem in the field while providing a unified proof for all dimensions $n \ge 4$. To prove uniqueness at this endpoint, we develop an averaged trace norm method, which combines complex geometrical optics with trace-norm estimates averaged over directions.

papers.title: One pool, many targets: a conservation layer and what archival data can identify
papers.abstract: Pairwise guide-transcript scores do not enforce conservation of a finite guide-loaded RISC pool when they are interpreted independently as occupancies. We formulate a differentiable scalar equilibrium layer: one conservation equation with a unique positive root and exact implicit gradients. It yields a redistribution theorem, a qualified high-resource limit, an analysis of the retrieval approximation, and a conditional rank-invariance result: within one construct at one dose, rankings by fractional occupancy cannot distinguish equilibrium from independent scoring. We therefore audit the two experiments that proposition leaves open, dose and cross-context, on archival off-target data. Corrected thermodynamic affinities associate weakly with measured repression in the direction a working predictor requires, but a paired permutation test and a construct-cluster bootstrap do not establish added predictive value from the coupling: what survives their differing permutation-null baselines is 0.0026, which is 2.55 paired-null standard deviations from that baseline (p=0.010) and favours independent scoring. The dose fits are heterogeneous and frequently violate the model-implied exponent constraint, which is superlinear rather than sublinear, so these data do not identify the competition parameter. A saturable compression of the competitor set holds both accuracy targets on held-out guide families but is not faster at the size measured. The contribution is a reusable conservation operator and the experimental information needed to test it. Code, result files and the data manifest: https://github.com/shadi97kh/One-Pool-Many-Targets

papers.title: Spike-driven Vision-Language-Action Model
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models bridge multimodal understanding and robotic control, advancing the dominant paradigm for embodied intelligence. However, most existing models rely on large Transformers, whose latency and energy costs hinder deployment on resource-constrained platforms. Through sparse event-driven computation, spiking neural networks offer a promising paradigm for high-performance and energy-efficient computing. Here, we propose the first Spike-driven VLA framework enabling end-to-end direct training for robotic manipulation, which mainly comprises three core components. First, we develop spiking visual and instruction encoders for multimodal perception, encoding visual observations and language instructions into sparse, reliable spike representations for subsequent cross-modal fusion. Then, we introduce Multi-Winner Spike Fusion for instruction-guided scene understanding, using bidirectional top-$k$ winner-take-all spike routing to suppress background interference and yield fused memory. Finally, we propose a Spike Action Chunking Transformer that incorporates spiking cross-attention over the fused memory and the current robot state, enabling efficient end-to-end generation of continuous action chunks for robotic control. Extensive experiments on LIBERO and Meta-World demonstrate that Spike-driven VLA achieves competitive performance with fewer parameters and lower estimated inference energy than conventional VLA models. This work establishes a foundational framework for neuromorphic VLA modeling, paving the way for future advances in resource-efficient embodied intelligence.

papers.title: ElectrolyteFM: Unifying Electrolyte Property Prediction through Cross-Property Knowledge Learning
papers.abstract: Electrolyte formulation design requires balancing multiple physicochemical properties, yet existing models often focus on a limited subset. Learning each property in isolation can overlook transferable chemical information, whereas indiscriminate sharing can introduce cross-property interference. Our directed transfer analysis shows that jointly learning two property prediction tasks can improve or degrade prediction relative to separate training, with asymmetric transfer effects between the tasks. We propose ElectrolyteFM, a unified multi-property prediction model which can more accurately predict multiple properties of each electrolyte by effectively identifying and utilizing property-specific features and knowledge shared across properties. More specifically, ElectrolyteFM learns property-specific representations independently and captures cross-property knowledge through a separately trained expert pool. A router selects relevant shared information for each formulation and target property, and property-specific residual adapters convert this information into corrections to the corresponding representation for prediction. Experiments on Electrolyte12 show that ElectrolyteFM reduces normalized mean absolute error averaged across 12 electrolyte properties by 14.8% relative to the strongest electrolyte-specific baseline. On an independent sodium-electrolyte dataset unseen during training, it reduces conductivity mean absolute error by 6.7% relative to the best-performing baseline.

papers.title: Matisse: Evidence-Space Reasoning for Active 3D Reconstruction
papers.abstract: How can a 3D reconstruction system acquire and retain useful information to understand the geometry of a scene from partial views under a limited computation budget? Existing active view acquisition methods typically estimate uncertainty over observed or instantiated geometry, limiting their ability to reason about unseen structure, while long-horizon reconstruction methods often retain redundant observations. We introduce Matisse, a training-free framework that unifies active reconstruction and keyframe selection by leveraging evidence provided by a pretrained generative 3D model. Matisse estimates Evidential Uncertainty from cross-attention evidence associated with 3D latent tokens and derives an Evidential Information Gain to guide both view acquisition and keyframe selection based on the expected reduction in posterior entropy. Matisse supports multi-object scenes through occlusion-aware, object-balanced aggregation and propagates uncertainty through intermediate latents to avoid full reconstruction during planning. Matisse reduces Chamfer distance by 12.7%, 3.8%, and 9.2% on GSO30, YCB-V, and Replica, respectively, relative to the best baseline on each dataset, and achieves a $1.50\times$ end-to-end speedup over the best active reconstruction baseline on GSO30 with the same backend. In the GSO30 keyframe selection experiment for long-horizon reconstruction, Matisse achieves 18.3% lower Chamfer distance than Stream3D and approaches convergence using roughly 20% as many views.

papers.title: Code4Scene: Benchmarking Coding Agents for Constructing and Editing 3D Scenes
papers.abstract: Frontier coding agents can now write and execute code that authors 3D environments, but whether they reliably understand 3D structure and precisely control scene state remains unclear. The generated 3D scene is a persistent, executable artifact: a convincing render can hide incorrect spatial relations, intersecting objects, or unintended modifications. We introduce Code4Scene, a benchmark of 170 Unreal Engine cases built from human-assembled scenes that evaluates coding agents on two complementary settings under a shared execution interface. Construction tests scene-level spatial reasoning from open-ended language specifications, where many realizations are valid; editing tests precise control of scene state, where the agent must recover the target scene from reference images while preserving everything else. Rather than scoring code or rendered views, Code4Scene evaluates the generated engine-native scene for task fulfillment, artifact integrity, and static physical validity, with edits additionally compared against withheld ground truth. Across 14 coding-agent systems on the 83-case public set, construction and editing performance are strongly correlated but not interchangeable (Spearman $ρ= 0.67$): Claude Fable 5.1 leads construction, Gemini 3.8 Flash leads editing. Spatial Composition is the weakest construction category for every agent, while editing remains imprecise: the best Repair F1 is only 0.562, and 34.2% of edits that fully recover the target still introduce unintended changes elsewhere in the scene. These results expose a gap between plausible 3D generation and reliable spatial reasoning and state control. The project webpage is at https://simworld.org/code4scene.

papers.title: Where Root Cause Analysis Fails: A Retrieval-Reranking Decomposition
papers.abstract: Identifying the root cause of an anomaly among hundreds of sensors is critical for preventing safety incidents and costly downtime in complex monitored systems. Existing studies evaluate root cause analysis (RCA) methods using top@k accuracy. We show that this metric has a fundamental blind spot: it conflates two failure modes, retrieval failure, where the true cause is never considered, and reranking failure, where it is considered but ranked too low. In this work, we introduce a retrieval-reranking decomposition and audit four well-known benchmarks to expose this blind spot. Our experiments show that, on industrial CPS benchmarks, the statistical baseline scoring every sensor mis-ranks the true cause 79-100% of the time, and graph-based methods never clearly beat the best statistical baseline, whether their causal graphs are learned on short fault windows, on retrieved candidate pools guaranteed to contain the cause, or on multi-day normal-operation data. Meanwhile, on microservice benchmarks, where each injected fault drives the faulty service's own metric far above its baseline, retrieval is nearly solved (98-100%). Guided by the decomposition, we build a two-stage pipeline combining a multi-signal retriever with an LLM reranker that, as one fixed configuration, matches or exceeds the best baseline's top@1 accuracy on all six benchmark suites (by up to +12 points), with no causal graph or labeled data required. When all methods rank the same retrieved candidates with the true cause guaranteed present, adding a short system-description document lets the reranker lead the best baseline by +7 to +18 points on every benchmark. Code is available at https://github.com/cruiseresearchgroup/DecompRCA.

papers.title: When Semantics Matter: Reliability-Aware Semantic-Rhythm Control for Co-Speech Gesture Generation
papers.abstract: Co-speech gesture generation aims to synthesize natural gestures that are both temporally synchronized with speech and semantically consistent with the spoken content. Although recent methods can generate rhythmically plausible motions, they often rely heavily on acoustic prosody while underutilizing textual semantics, especially when semantic annotations are incomplete, noisy, or unavailable. Consequently, the generated gestures may follow speech rhythm while failing to express the intended semantics. To address this problem, we propose a reliability-aware semantic-rhythm control framework for co-speech gesture generation. We first learn a discrete motion prior that represents continuous gestures in a compact and structured motion-code space. We then introduce a dual-branch semantic contribution estimation mechanism consisting of a full multimodal branch and an audio-only branch. Their distributional discrepancy provides a model-based proxy for text-induced predictive influence, which is interpreted jointly with segment-level semantic relevance. Based on this estimate, a controllable semantic-rhythm objective selectively strengthens semantic guidance in content-relevant segments while limiting unnecessary semantic intervention in rhythm-dominant segments. Furthermore, we treat background noise as an acoustic reliability condition and introduce noise-conditioned feature modulation together with benefit-regularized latent perturbation to improve generation robustness under realistic acoustic environments. Experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves a favorable balance among semantic expressiveness, rhythmic synchronization, motion diversity, and robustness, enabling reliable and controllable co-speech gesture generation.

papers.title: On intersection forms of spin $4$-manifolds with AR homology sphere boundary
papers.abstract: In this paper, building on the work of Dai--Sasahira--Stoffregen, we derive constraints on the intersection forms of smooth, compact, indefinite, spin $4$-manifolds bounded by almost-rational plumbed homology spheres (AR homology spheres) using two methods. First, we use the constraints on the existence of $\operatorname{Pin}(2)$-equivariant maps between representation spheres, established by Hopkins--Lin--Shi--Xu in their proof of the $10/8 + 4$-inequality. Second, we compute Lin's $κo$-invariant for AR homology spheres. Combined with Lin's version of the relative $10/8$-inequality, this computation yields constraints different from those based on Hopkins--Lin--Shi--Xu. As applications, we give an alternative proof of the non-sliceness of the $(2n, 1)$-cables of the figure-eight knot for even $n$---a result originally proved by Kang, Park, and Taniguchi via real Seiberg--Witten theory---by showing within ordinary Seiberg--Witten theory that certain cyclic branched covers of them are nontrivial in the homology cobordism group. We also obtain new lower bounds on the minimal genus of surfaces in various $4$-manifolds bounded by knots whose double branched covers are AR homology spheres. Moreover, we provide an obstruction to smooth $4$-manifold decompositions related to the $11/8$-conjecture.

papers.title: On Talagrand Type
papers.abstract: We prove that for every $1<s<2$ and every $0<δ<1$, Rademacher type $s$ coincides with Talagrand type $(s,ψ_{s,δ})$. Together with the result of Cordero-Erausquin and Eskenazis for $s=2$, this yields the equivalence for every $1<s\le2$ and every $0<δ<1$.

papers.title: OpenWhistle: A Large-Scale Longitudinal Dataset and Benchmark of Bottlenose Dolphin Vocalizations
papers.abstract: Recent advances in bioacoustics have been driven by large-scale corpora and standardized benchmarks, yet existing resources are overwhelmingly bird-centric and shallow per species, limiting their use for studying the structure of a single species' communication system. This gap is particularly acute for cetaceans: despite bottlenose dolphins (Tursiops truncatus) being a compelling case of complex vocal communication among non-human mammals, existing dolphin datasets are small, fragmented, and largely closed. We introduce OpenWhistle, the largest publicly available dataset of dolphin vocalizations. It comprises approximately 180,000 whistles (114 hours) recorded over five years from a stable pod of five individuals in a semi-natural environment, paired with a curated subset of 8,354 expert-annotated whistles and reproducible evaluation protocols for whistle-type detection and classification. We further release the full processing pipeline for whistle detection, segmentation, and categorization. To demonstrate its utility, we pretrain a Wav2Vec2.0 model adapted to dolphin acoustics on the OpenWhistle corpus and show that it learns effective representations, outperforming general-purpose bioacoustic models such as AVES and BioLingual on both tasks while leaving meaningful headroom for future work. By releasing the dataset, pipeline, and evaluation protocol, we provide the first open dolphin whistle dataset tailored for training self-supervised models, laying the groundwork for advancing dolphin communication research and developing models that capture fine-grained acoustic structure within species.

papers.title: The Dynamical Radius of Comparison for C*-Dynamical Systems
papers.abstract: We introduce a dynamical version $\operatorname{rc} (A, α)$ of the radius of comparison $\operatorname{rc} (A)$ of a unital C*-algebra, based on the dynamical Cuntz semigroup. We also give an intrinsic ordered semigroup definition, which agrees with $\operatorname{rc} (A, α)$ when $A$ is residually stably finite, and is lower semicontinuous for equivariant direct limits with injective unital maps. We construct actions $α$ of $G = \mathbb{Z} / 2 \mathbb{Z}$ on simple unital AH~algebras for which $\operatorname{rc} (A, α)$ lies strictly between $\operatorname{rc} (A)$ and $\operatorname{rc} (A) / \operatorname{card} (G)$, and actions $α$ of a finite group $G$ on unital C*-algebras for which $\operatorname{rc} (A, α)$ lies strictly between $\operatorname{rc} (A)$ and $\operatorname{rc} (C^* (G, A, α))$. For a minimal action of a countable discrete group $G$ on a zero dimensional compact metrizable space $X$, and with $α$ being the corresponding action on $C (X)$, we prove that $\operatorname{rc} (C (X), α) = 0$ if and only if the action on~$X$ has dynamical comparison as defined by Kerr. For finite group actions on simple unital stably finite C*-algebras, assuming the weak tracial Rokhlin property, we get $\operatorname{rc} (A, α) \leq \operatorname{rc} (A) / \operatorname{card} (G)$, and assuming weak tracial strict approximate innerness, we get $\operatorname{rc} (A, α) = \operatorname{rc} (A)$.

papers.title: A finitely generated Linear group without property (T) that is neither inner amenable nor properly proximal
papers.abstract: We construct an explicit finitely generated ICC subgroup of $\operatorname{GL}_4(\mathbb{F}_2(t))$ that is neither inner amenable nor properly proximal and does not have Kazhdan's property (T). The group is obtained by adjoining a scalar dilation to Caprace's example. In particular, this has resolved a question due to Boutonnet, Ioana, and Peterson in negative.

papers.title: A Diagnostic Method for Proto-Neutron Star Magnetic Fields by Supernova Fallback Neutrinos
papers.abstract: Young isolated neutron stars exhibit a wide range of magnetic field strengths. To understand the origin of this diversity, it is important to observationally constrain magnetic fields during the proto-neutron star (PNS) phase. We propose a novel diagnostic of PNS magnetic fields using neutrinos associated with supernova fallback. By performing one-dimensional general-relativistic magnetohydrodynamic simulations of the supernova fallback onto a magnetized PNS, we investigate how the energy spectra of the fallback neutrinos depend on the PNS magnetic field strength and the fallback accretion rate. We find that stronger magnetic fields and lower accretion rates produce softer spectra because the fallback neutrinos are emitted mainly near the magnetospheric radius, which becomes larger under these conditions. To quantify this spectral softening, we define a hardness ratio based on event rates above and below 30 MeV and introduce a hardness-event-rate diagram. Using this diagram, we identify the parameter region in which our diagnostic is applicable. Its applicability depends on the PNS magnetic field strength, fallback accretion rate, onset time of the fallback phase, and neutrino mass ordering. We also investigate the dependence on the PNS radius and find that a larger radius produces softer spectra, indicating a degeneracy between the magnetic field and PNS compactness. An independent constraint on the PNS compactness would therefore enable us to better constrain the magnetic field. These results suggest that future multimessenger observations of galactic supernovae can provide a new window into the NS diversity.

papers.title: FlowMLLab: An open-source framework for reproducible computational-fluid-dynamics and scientific-machine-learning experiments
papers.abstract: FlowMLLab is an open-source Python framework for scientific machine learning in thermal-fluid and aerospace engineering, covering incompressible, compressible and rarefied flows. Its 22 weeks comprise 51 notebooks and 35 lectures. Solvers and molecular sampling underpin field prediction, uncertainty quantification and reduced-order modeling. Proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) and deep operator networks (DeepONets), including POD-DeepONet, connect operating conditions to flow fields alongside Fourier neural operators. Physics-informed neural networks infer solutions and constitutive coefficients. Geometry-conditioned models, including the point-cloud DeepONet variant Geom-DeepONet, handle changing domains. Aerospace applications address airfoil shock/vortex identification, rarefied-gas modeling, nozzle flow prediction and supersonic body design. Complementary thermal-fluid examples cover unsteady wakes, hydrofoil vapor clouds and noisy particle observations. Attention mechanisms support sparse-sensor reconstruction, autoregressive prediction and transfer assessment, alongside character-level language modeling. Complete-case evaluation excludes tests from selection; execution notes identify retained research outputs. A worked extension embeds a learned monotone relation for a fixed manufactured Carreau fluid in channel momentum balance. At three unseen in-support pressure gradients, it outperforms profile-interpolation and fitted-Newtonian controls with different information or priors.

papers.title: Modular integrals for individual modular knots
papers.abstract: To each modular knot, we attach a weight $2$ modular integral for $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$ whose homogenized cycle integrals recover its linking numbers with other modular knots in $S^3$. This construction answers Choie-Zagier's question of explicitly constructing modular integrals with given rational period functions in weight $2$. Our formula applies to individual modular knots without symmetrization, thereby realizing an approach discussed but not pursued by Duke-Imamoglu-Tóth. This gives an answer to Ghys' question on pairwise linking numbers in terms of modular integrals, as sought by Simon.

papers.title: Regular Cosmologies: Three Distinct Routes
papers.abstract: Regular black holes avoid the central singularity by replacing it with a de Sitter core. We ask what cosmology follows if the same idea is brought to the early universe. Regular metrics define a position-dependent cosmological term, $Λ_{\rm eff}(r)=8πG ρ_{\rm MS}(r)$, and there is no unique way to carry it over to the expanding universe. We follow three different prescriptions: a Newtonian one following McCrea and Milne, a running vacuum evaluated at Hubble radius and a quasi-local one based on Misner-Sharp mass. We apply each of them to six regular black hole metrics and explore their consequences. In the Newtonian case the Friedmann equations are solved in closed form for the Hayward metric, and in terms of standard special functions or numerically for the others, and describe a universe that starts in a de Sitter phase and ends as dust (i.e. an inflationary model instead of dark energy). We find that in all three prescriptions a monotonically decreasing core density gives an equation of state that never crosses $w=-1$, and thus the phantom behaviour suggested by DESI would require a density shell which a regular core does not have. The three prescriptions agree on the de Sitter core but differ at late times, and we quantify the difference against the DESI DR2 results. We also point out that a single regularisation length cannot serve as both the inflationary and the dark-energy scale.

papers.title: Flux: Optimal Scheduling of Optical Circuit Switches for LLM Training
papers.abstract: Optical Circuit Switching (OCS) offers high bandwidth density and energy efficiency for LLM training, but incurs a non-negligible reconfiguration delay. Prior work typically schedules optical circuit switches independently of compute, using aggregate traffic demand to determine which circuits to provision and when. We argue that this separation creates a fundamental inefficiency: reconfigurations that ignore the compute timeline can stall communication, resulting in low circuit utilization and large buffer requirements. In this paper, we present Flux, a scheduler that optimally schedules optical circuit switches based on the structure of the entire workload. Flux remains effective across a wide range of switching speeds by reusing circuits and amortizing reconfiguration delay behind compute and communication. We show that Flux reduces training iteration time by up to $10\times$ and peak NIC buffer requirements by more than three orders of magnitude compared to traditional periodic schedulers.

papers.title: rApp/xApp Attestation: A New Security Use Case for O-RAN
papers.abstract: The disaggregation and softwarization introduced by the Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN) architecture enable multi-vendor innovation but also expose the RAN Intelligent Controller (RIC) ecosystem to new runtime security risks. Existing O-RAN specifications define strong safeguards for onboarding, authentication, identity management, and secure communication; however, they do not provide a concrete mechanism for verifying whether deployed rApps and xApps remain in their intended, untampered state during operation. This paper introduces rApp/xApp attestation as a RIC-native O-RAN security use case for runtime integrity verification. Rather than proposing a new cryptographic protocol, the work defines how existing integrity verification techniques can be integrated into O-RAN through attestation modules, attestation agents, RIC application interfaces, and SMO-driven policy coordination. We map the use case to relevant O-RAN Alliance working groups, identify required standardization extensions, and demonstrate feasibility through a lightweight hash-based prototype implemented on the Near-RT RIC platform. Experimental results show attestation latencies below 40 ms across multiple cryptographic hash functions, indicating that runtime attestation can be performed without disrupting time-sensitive RIC operations when appropriately scheduled. Finally, we discuss remaining technical and standardization challenges, including trusted verification, known-good runtime states, scalability, mitigation policies, and future hybrid attestation mechanisms.

papers.title: FLARE: A Full-Lifecycle Dense Supervision Paradigm for Long-Horizon Coding Agents via Generative Reward Model
papers.abstract: While test-time scaling enhances Large Language Model (LLM) agents in long-horizon software engineering (SWE), sparse binary rewards (Pass/Fail) create a severe credit assignment crisis and waste failed exploratory trajectories. Current trajectory optimization and scaling methods are costly and structurally limited, relying on heuristic state reuse without causal diagnosis or delayed scalar scoring without actionable online guidance. We propose FLARE (Full-Lifecycle Alignment and Reward Engine), a novel dense supervision paradigm driven by a lightweight Generative Reward Model (GRM). First, RADAR, an offline causal-aware diagnostic framework, extracts high-fidelity, hindsight-free supervision through causal-chain backtracking to distill a GRM providing real-time, step-level risk feedback. Second, FLARE uses this GRM to continuously optimize the agent across its entire lifecycle. During inference, FLARE acts as an Active Scaffold, autonomously intercepting high-risk generation steps for localized breakpoint re-execution, drastically reducing compute overhead. During post-training, the GRM's structured signals serve as process-supervised reranking scores for Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and step-level dense rewards for Reinforcement Learning (RL), mitigating policy collapse in sparse environments. Extensive evaluations show that FLARE establishes a new Pareto frontier across the agent lifecycle: FLARE (N=1) outperforms Global Rollout (N=5) with a 5x reduction in token consumption. Extending FLARE to training overcomes the sparse reward problem in long-horizon interactive tasks, delivering relative performance gains of 19.13% in SFT through process-aware data curation and a consistent 9.19% improvement in RL.

papers.title: RPMem: Learning Long-Term Recurrent Parametric Memory Across Sessions for LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Long-running LLM agents require memory that persists and evolves across sessions. Text-based memory retrieves and reconstructs past interactions at every query, making long-horizon performance increasingly dependent on retrieval quality and contextual reasoning as histories grow. Parametric memory encodes experience directly into model computation, but existing approaches provide limited support for cross-session memory evolution. Their coupling to a specific backbone further restricts memory reuse after model replacement. We introduce RPMem, a two-stage architecture that compiles each session into a model-independent latent memory through forward computation and selectively integrates it with retained memory via a task-trained recurrent gate. The consolidated memory is then mapped to backbone-specific low-rank adaptation (LoRA) parameters, allowing the encoding capability to transfer when the backbone is replaced. Evaluation across three long-term memory benchmarks and five diverse backbones demonstrates broad generalization with near-constant update cost and memory footprint. With Qwen3-8B on PERMA, RPMem reaches 85.52%, outperforming the strongest parametric and text-based baselines by 5.32 and 12.98 percentage points, respectively. Ablations validate the complementary roles of session compilation and cross-session consolidation, while dynamics analyses reveal that the gate acquires task-specific memory integration strategies. These results establish RPMem as a lifecycle-independent parametric memory framework that maintains evolving cross-session memory that remains reusable across backbone replacements. Our code is available at https://github.com/Quark-Medical/rpmem/tree/main.

papers.title: On an inverse boundary problem in elastodynamics
papers.abstract: We study the simultaneous identification of the Lamé parameters $λ$ and $μ$ in three-dimensional static isotropic elasticity. For smooth coefficients, we establish uniqueness from the full Dirichlet-to-Neumann map when $μ$ is axisymmetric, admits a multiplicative or additive separation on a product domain, or is quasianalytic in one fixed direction. These results require neither smallness of $\nablaμ$ nor real analyticity of the coefficients, and impose no corresponding structural condition on $λ$. In the axisymmetric and separated cases, partial boundary data suffice to determine $μ$.

papers.title: VibeAvatar: Aligning Phonetic Kinematics and Human Aesthetics for High-Fidelity Talking Avatar Synthesis
papers.abstract: Multi-modal talking avatar synthesis aims to generate realistic talking videos from a reference portrait and speech. Despite rapid progress in diffusion-based methods, existing approaches still struggle to jointly achieve accurate lip articulation, human-preferred motion aesthetics, and efficient inference. We observe that phonetic accuracy and motion aesthetics arise from fundamentally different sources and should be addressed at complementary stages rather than learned implicitly by a single generator. Based on this insight, we propose VibeAvatar, which disentangles these two objectives through a Phonetic Kinematics Adapter (PKA) that converts recognition-oriented speech features into phonetic-kinematic conditions at the conditioning stage, and an Aesthetic Motion Policy (AMP) that optimizes a flow-consistent stochastic sampling policy via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) at the post-training stage. With a lightweight flow-based motion generator operating in a compact 1D warp-based latent motion space, VibeAvatar achieves state-of-the-art results in articulation, aesthetics, and efficiency on both objective metrics and user studies, while generating a 10-second 512px video in under 10 seconds with only $\sim$3GB VRAM.

papers.title: Exact Replica-Sector Hierarchy of Multi-Resolvent Spectral-Weight Fluctuations in Random Free Fermions
papers.abstract: The one-point ETH envelope fixes the smooth part of a spectral density but not how the spectral weight of an eigenstate is distributed across channels; its higher-order correlations are joint fluctuations of those weights and are carried by connected products of channel resolvents. In random free fermions every channel overlap is a squared Slater minor of a Haar-orthogonal one-body eigenvector matrix, and the multi-resolvent hierarchy has an exact microscopic realization there. The $r$-resolvent moment admits a decomposition into finitely many overlap sectors whose values are fixed by the channel and eigenstate overlap patterns and whose weights are exact finite-$N$ orthogonal Weingarten functions: the sector theorem holds at arbitrary finite multiplicity, it is realized in full at $r=3$ ($k=2,3,4$) and through exact sector slices at $r=4,5$, and the sector moments lift to connected resolvent cumulants and to the irreducible Feshbach self-energy vertices, whose deep plane begins at the order $z^{-(3r-2)}$. At $r=2$ this structure reproduces and completes an exact benchmark in which a flat envelope coexists with a non-Porter--Thomas intensity hierarchy and closes the two-resolvent covariance, and under interaction it separates into a deep plane fixed by Hamiltonian channel moments and a bulk that requires eigenstate-resolved information.

papers.title: Structure Across Voices: Comparing acoustic-event type accumulation and sequence dependence across four vocal corpora using frozen audio encoders
papers.abstract: Comparing acoustic structure across very different vocal corpora is difficult because the recordings use different native event units, contain different amounts of sequence, and were collected under different conditions. We use the high-dimensional representations of frozen, pretrained audio encoders to measure acoustic diversity and temporal organization. Matched sampling gives each corpus the same opportunities to observe new acoustic forms and relationships between events, without changing its native event definition. We compare sperm-whale codas, human speech phones, Bengalese-finch syllables, and common-marmoset calls using 1,952 events and 1,700 adjacent pairs per comparison. Whale shows the fastest accumulation of encoder-defined acoustic groups, while Finch has the strongest repeated-sequence recurrence against ordinary within-block shuffles. Their neighboring-event dependence is closely matched under a source-and-position control. A second preceding event changes held-out prediction more favorably for Whale than for the other corpora, although Whale's standalone improvement remains uncertain. Waveform measurements recover several differences, but duration and acquisition-sensitive properties also contribute. Together, the findings show how pretrained representations can measure distinct forms of vocal organization, while waveform and source controls define the scope of the comparison.

papers.title: Convex Order and Moment Persuasion
papers.abstract: We study Bayesian persuasion with multidimensional states when the sender's payoff depends on the distribution of posterior means. The choice of information policy in such an environment reduces to an optimization over distributions of posterior means dominated by the prior in convex order. We study extreme points of this feasible set using results on irreducible-component structure from martingale transport theory.
