We further characterize the explicit forms of these transformations and establish a transport theorem describing how twisted conjugation acts on the supports and multipliers of GRS codes. These results provide an algebraic framework for constructing and analyzing induced centrosymmetric alternant codes.

papers.title: IH-Benchmark: A Conflict-Centered Benchmark for Instruction-Hierarchy Robustness in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: When a language model receives conflicting instructions from different priority levels, which one does it actually follow? This question lies at the heart of reliable LLM deployment. Existing benchmarks answer this only partially, often focusing on a single hierarchy component or adapting public datasets with limited tool-use coverage. We present IH-Benchmark, a conflict-centered benchmark for instruction-hierarchy robustness across direct System $\succ$ User (S $\succ$ U) conflicts and tool-mediated User $\succ$ Tool (U $\succ$ T) conflicts. We organize tests into seven constraint categories according to the higher-priority requirements under evaluation. Each test is evaluated with a uniform binary pass/fail protocol combining a predicate domain-specific language (DSL) with rubric-based LLM judges. We report category-balanced compliance rates and evaluate non-conflict controls separately. Our evaluation of 32 model configurations over five runs each reveals substantial variation in overall compliance, with scores ranging from 32.9% to 97.8%. Models achieve higher compliance on S $\succ$ U than on U $\succ$ T on average, at 84.6% and 69.6%, respectively. Strong performance on the former track does not guarantee comparable robustness on the latter. Constraint hardening provides a prompt-based defense, but its benefits depend on the model and how conflicting instructions are delivered. Several models also resist unauthorized tool actions more reliably than injected instructions that alter response language or factual content. Together, these results show that high aggregate compliance can conceal weaknesses in specific conflict tracks and instruction requirements. We release IH-Benchmark, including the benchmark corpus, agent simulators, and evaluation harness, at LINK_RELEASE_AFTER_PEER_REVIEW.

papers.title: Gravitational Wave Modeling of White-Dwarf--Compact-Object Binaries and Observational Outlook
papers.abstract: Binaries consisting of a white dwarf and a compact object (neutron stars, black holes, or sub-solar-mass compact objects) display unique orbital evolution and gravitational wave signals. We investigate the end stages of these systems by developing a novel integrator implementing mass transfer and 2.5-order Post-Newtonian kinematics. White-dwarf--compact-object binaries are subject to two phases: a slow inspiral during which binary evolution is dominated by weak-gravity radiation reaction and a quicker "outspiral" dominated by mass transfer. These systems have unique gravitational waveforms with several characteristic features including an accumulation of signal near the maximum cutoff frequency set by the transition between in- and outspiral. We investigate trends in gravitational wave parameters based on component masses. In particular, maximum cutoff frequency depends strongly on white dwarf mass and compactness. It is unlikely that extragalactic binaries will be measured by LISA or current or future terrestrial detectors. However, white-dwarf--compact-object binary end stages will be an important source for future decihertz detectors such as DECIGO and LGWA: The final inspiral of tens of white-dwarf--neutron-star binaries will be detected annually by LGWA, and millions of inspirals along with thousands of outspirals will be detected by DECIGO. The ultimate fates of these binaries are diverse and dependent upon the intricacies of angular momentum loss. In particular, we show that white dwarfs with partners of sufficiently low/high mass can end their lives in mergers, while white dwarfs do not enter contact with partners of intermediate mass. The highest frequencies produced by white-dwarf--compact-object binaries in our tests are 10--20 Hz--incapable of mimicking sub-solar-mass compact object signals in terrestrial detectors or explaining S251112cm-like signals.

papers.title: Test-Time Coverage: Test-Conditioned Data Curation for Deployment-Aware Learning
papers.abstract: Deployed AI systems are often trained from broad candidate data pools, necessitating data curation towards the deployment test distribution. However, standard data curation methods score training-side criteria rather than directly optimizing deployment match. We introduce TTCov (Test-Time Coverage), a data-level test-conditioned curation method that uses test-side information before training instead of updating model weights at inference. TTCov decomposes deployment-conditioned curation into coverage and distribution. To represent coverage, it builds a task Atlas, a collection of LLM-based atomic propositions (APs) describing deployment-relevant concepts, seeded from open task knowledge and expanded with unmatched APs extracted from unlabeled deployment samples. To represent distribution, it instantiates the matched deployment APs with their frequencies, yielding a Knowledge Atlas (K-Atlas) that operationalizes the deployment distribution as a curation target. TTCov then selects a budgeted training set whose deployment APs distribution approximates this target. We apply TTCov towards autonomous driving (AD), keeping adaptation off the inference path while selecting data with greater deployment-relevant coverage, closer K-Atlas matching, and stronger downstream end-to-end driving performance than data-curation baselines, including seamless adaptability to novel domains via city-to-city expansion. Code available at https://github.com/NVlabs/TTCov.

papers.title: Offline Preference-Based Trajectory Evaluation
papers.abstract: Offline evaluation of agentic systems often collapses trajectories into a binary terminal success value, discarding information about partial progress. This, in turn, results in widespread ties that create statistical inefficiency by reducing effective sample size and weakening the ability to distinguish systems. We propose preference-based trajectory evaluation, an evaluation measure that compares pairs of trajectories directly by using temporal preferences between time-to-return profiles. We find that, across diverse agentic and interactive benchmarks, success-based metrics result in tied comparisons on roughly 75% of instances, while trajectory-aware preferences reduce ties to roughly 35%, improving discriminative power, ranking stability, and data efficiency. Our results suggest that benchmark saturation, often portrayed as the result of poor data collection or problem difficulty, may also be explained by the design of the evaluation measure.

papers.title: Students' Validation Criteria for AI-Generated Physics Solutions
papers.abstract: A physics solution can be clear without being valid. This distinction becomes important when students read AI-generated solutions that appear coherent but still require physical and mathematical checking. We examined how pre-service physics teachers in a calculus-based introductory electromagnetism course evaluated AI-generated solutions to a charged-rod electric-field problem after attempting the problem themselves. Although the AI-generated solutions analyzed were correct, no student accepted a response as valid after a first reading. Students who had solved the problem fully or in part could examine the responses using physical and mathematical criteria, while others withheld acceptance because they could not follow the mathematical development. These results suggest that, in physics instruction, AI-generated solutions should be treated less as answers to be accepted or rejected and more as worked-out responses that students learn to reconstruct, question, and test.

papers.title: Beyond the probabilistic scaling for NLS on the ball
papers.abstract: We construct probabilistic strong solutions to the cubic Schrödinger equation on the three-dimensional ball with radial initial data, which is a significant improvement of a result by Bourgain--Bulut. These solutions lie in the supercritical regime with respect to the probabilistic scaling introduced by Deng--Nahmod--Yue. We achieve this result through gauge transformations, without renormalization, combined with a refined modulation analysis using random averaging operators.

papers.title: What Am I Missing? Question-Answering as Hidden State Probing
papers.abstract: The study of test-time reasoning in large language models (LLMs) has attracted increasing interests due to its profound impact on many tasks, with early work tracing back to approaches such as chain-of-thought reasoning. The basic mechanism underlying the test-time reasoning process, however, is still under-studied: from the same input prompt, and even the same partial solution, LLMs can produce varied answers if sampled multiple times. In this paper, we leverage question-asking as an inference-time intervention that articulates information about the model's hidden state. Specifically, we present a student-teacher setting where a student asks questions to a teacher. We train a probe on the student's hidden state before and after asking a question and find it is predictive of the trajectory's final correctness, even before generating the teacher's answer. This suggests there is a meaningful signal from the self-diagnosis that occurs during question generation rather than information transfer from the teacher. We then frame question-asking as a sequential decision problem, using this probe as a quality score, and define a gating policy to ask questions that maximize likelihood of correctness. We find that the success of question-asking as an intervention is largely dependent on the model's self-consistency. Our empirical results show a gap between detection and recovery; while our gating policy captures model correctness and uncertainty, interventions are equally likely to harm correct trajectories as they are to recover incorrect ones. This gap between diagnosis and correction has broader implications on language models' capacity for self-refinement under uncertainty.

papers.title: Supervised Training Rapidly Degrades Early Visual Cortex Alignment Across Biologically Plausible Learning Rules
papers.abstract: CORRECTION (August 2026): the central finding of this paper is not supported. An evaluation-mode defect left the batch-normalisation layers of the predictive-coding and STDP conditions in training mode during feature extraction, producing their apparent preservation of V1 alignment. With the defect repaired, predictive coding degrades V1 alignment more than backpropagation does, not less. The finding that training degrades V1 alignment for every rule tested does survive. [Revision note: not robust to the analysis choices examined in arXiv:2611.15533.] See the correction note on page 1; the original abstract below and the body are unchanged from v1. Corrected analysis: arXiv:2608.12408. Revision note: see Comments. Random, untrained neural networks consistently match or exceed trained networks in representational similarity to early visual cortex. This puzzling finding challenges the assumption that learning improves brain alignment. We investigate it by tracking representational similarity analysis (RSA) alignment to human fMRI data across training for four learning rules: backpropagation (BP), feedback alignment (FA), predictive coding (PC), and spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP). Using 720 object images from the THINGS database and fMRI data from three subjects across six visual ROIs, we measure Spearman correlations between model and brain representational dissimilarity matrices at eight training checkpoints (epochs 0-40). We find that (1) a single epoch of training reduces V1 alignment by 25-90%, depending on the learning rule; (2) backpropagation reduces V1 alignment most severely (delta r = -0.080), while predictive coding and STDP preserve substantially more (delta r ~ -0.04); and (3) a weaker, opposite tendency appears in object-selective cortex (LOC), where BP shows the largest increase in alignment during training, although the absolute change is small.

papers.title: Cross-Species RSA Reveals Conserved Early Visual Alignment but Divergent Higher-Area Rankings Across Human fMRI and Macaque Electrophysiology
papers.abstract: CORRECTION (August 2026): an evaluation-mode defect in the shared feature-extraction pipeline affected the predictive-coding and STDP conditions. It applies to both sides of every comparison here: the human values are reprinted from the companion study and the macaque values use the same checkpoints. In a single-seed re-evaluation with repaired checkpoints, macaque STDP at V1 moves from 0.305 to 0.266 and PC from 0.210 to 0.178, level with the untrained baseline, so finding (2) holds for STDP but not for PC; the V4 and IT orderings change, while V2 is unchanged. Revision note: the human V1 results are not robust to the analysis choices examined in arXiv:2611.15533. Findings (1), (3) and (4) are unaffected, and other conditions change by at most 0.0034. Five-seed analysis, tau, noise ceilings and stimulus control not re-computed. See the correction note on page 1; the abstract below is unchanged. Follow-up study: arXiv:2608.12408. Does the relationship between learning rules and brain alignment generalize across species? We test the same five learning rules against macaque electrophysiology. The macaque data come from MajajHong2015 (V4/IT, 3,200 presentations, 88/168 neurons) and FreemanZiemba2013 (V1/V2, 135 stimuli, 102/103 neurons). Using RSA with identical model weights from our human study, we find: (1) all models achieve higher alignment with macaque early visual cortex (rho = 0.15-0.30 at V1/V2) than with human fMRI (rho = 0.01-0.08); (2) STDP and PC produce the highest macaque V1/V2 alignment; (3) at IT, rankings show no detectable correlation across species (Kendall's tau = 0.00), though this null is expected given that n = 5 provides power only at tau = +/-1.0; (4) a pretrained ResNet-50 achieves rho = 0.25 at macaque IT, substantially above all custom CNN conditions (rho = 0.07-0.14), suggesting IT alignment is limited by model capacity rather than by the learning rule.

papers.title: DiffATS: Diffusion in Aligned Tensor Space
papers.abstract: Direct diffusion modeling of high-resolution spatiotemporal fields is computationally challenging. Parameter-efficient primitives address this by representing high-dimensional data with a compact set of parameters. In this paper, we construct data-dependent tensor primitives without pretrained compression autoencoders. Our construction starts from Tucker decomposition, which captures low-rank multilinear structure through a core tensor and mode-wise factors. However, Tucker factors are non-unique: the same tensor can be represented by different rotated factors, which complicates generative modeling. We address this issue with orthogonal Procrustes (OP) alignment. Specifically, we select medoid anchor matrices from the data and align the factor matrices to resolve the gauge ambiguity. This yields matrix Grassmannian primitives and tensor Grassmannian primitives that are compact, data-adaptive, and directly decodable by explicit multilinear reconstruction. Theoretically, we prove that the proposed primitive maps are homeomorphisms between low-rank tensors and their corresponding primitive spaces, certifying that the representations are non-degenerate and topologically faithful. Building on these primitives, we propose *Diffusion in Aligned Tensor Space* (DiffATS), a generative framework that trains diffusion models directly on aligned tensor primitives. Across images, videos, and PDE solutions, DiffATS achieves strong unconditional and conditional generation performance while compressing original data by $3.9\times$ to $210\times$, without relying on any pretrained deep compression autoencoders.

papers.title: A Closer Look on the Influence of Constraints Upon the Optimization of the Nonadditive Entropic Functional $S_{q}$
papers.abstract: The canonical distribution is obtained by maximizing the Boltzmann-Gibbs-von Neumann-Shannon entropy $S_{BG}(p)=k\sum^{W}_{i=1}p_{i}\ln 1/p_{i}$ constrained to $\sum^{W}_{i=1}p_{i}=1$ and $\sum^{W}_{i=1}p_{i}\,e_{i}=U$, $e_{1}\leq\ldots\leq e_{W}$ being the energies of the $W$ possible states and $U\in[e_{1},e_{W}]$ their mean value. We revisit a generalized version of this optimization problem grounded in the nonadditive entropy $S_{q}(p)=k\,(\sum^{W}_{i=1}p_{i}^{q}-1)/(1-q)$ (frequently, though not necessarily, $q\in(0,1)$; $S_1=S_{BG}$), and the constraint $\sum^{W}_{i=1} p_{i}^{q^{\prime}}e_{i} / \sum^{W}_{i=1}p_{i}^{q^{\prime}}=U$, $q^{\prime}>0$. Sufficient conditions for existence, strict positivity, and uniqueness of solutions are derived, along with a theorem that enables their closed-form calculation. We apply these results to deepen the understanding of the two standard cases in the literature ($q^{\prime}=1$ and $q^{\prime}=q$), as well as of a new one ($q^{\prime}=2-q$). We prove that these standard cases are the only ones yielding optimizing probability distributions of $q$-exponential form. Furthermore, we define an effective temperature $T_{q,q^{\prime}}$ through a Clausius-like relation $1/T_{q,q^{\prime}}=\partial S_{q} / \partial U$ and derive a Helmholtz-like energy $F_{q,q^{\prime}}=U-T_{q,q^{\prime}}S_{q}$, with the former grounding the validity of the $0^{\textrm{th}}$ Principle of Thermodynamics within this generalized statistical mechanics. Finally, we show that the case with a linear constraint (i.e., $q^{\prime}=1$) with $q\in(0,1)$ (i) preserves the Third Law of Thermodynamics; (ii) can be used to model classical many-body Hamiltonian systems with arbitrarily-ranged interactions; and (iii) resembles features of low-dimensional nonlinear dynamical systems at the edge of chaos.

papers.title: Scalable spin-nematic squeezing in multi-level dipole-interacting Rydberg atom arrays
papers.abstract: We study the dynamical generation of metrologically useful entanglement in arrays of three-level (spin-1) systems coupled by spin-exchange interactions, as realized by dipole-interacting Rydberg atoms in optical tweezers. We quantify the metrological gain by a generalized squeezing parameter optimized over all linear $\mathrm{SU}(3)$ phase generators and readout observables. For equal exchange couplings on the two transitions, the dynamics reduces to one-axis twisting (OAT) of an effective two-level system. Away from this point, the full three-level structure provides a genuine advantage. For all-to-all couplings, the optimal squeezing at $N=4000$ exceeds the OAT value by a factor of 3.6, with a fitted scaling exponent of $0.93$ compared with $0.69$ for OAT over $100\le N\le4000$. For two-dimensional dipolar arrays, exact and tensor-network simulations up to $N=49$ show that the optimal three-level protocol outperforms the effective spin-1/2 dynamics, with a gain that increases with system size, and semiclassical simulations show that squeezing continues to grow up to $N=10^4$. Crucially, our results demonstrate a real advantage of utilizing the full three-level $\mathrm{SU}(3)$ structure of the spin-1 system over $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ type one-axis twisting dynamics. Our results extend interaction-driven scalable squeezing beyond the well-studied qubit setting to spin-exchange-coupled qudits with dipolar interactions, and can be realized in current Rydberg tweezer experiments.

papers.title: Untrained CNNs Exceed Backpropagation in V1 Alignment at High Evaluation Resolution: A Systematic RSA Comparison of Four Learning Rules Against Human fMRI
papers.abstract: Revision note: the V1 result reported here is not robust to the analysis choices examined in arXiv:2611.15533; see page 1. We compare four learning rules (backpropagation (BP), feedback alignment (FA), predictive coding (PC), and spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP)) in identical convolutional networks against human fMRI from THINGS-fMRI (720 stimuli, 3 subjects) using representational similarity analysis (RSA), together with an untrained random-weights baseline that isolates the contribution of architecture. Models are trained on 32 px CIFAR-10 and evaluated at 224 px; results are averaged across 5 seeds, with uncertainty from resampling stimuli. At V1, the untrained baseline exceeds BP rho = 0.053$ vs. $0.022$; rho = +0.031$, 95% CI $[0.019, 0.043]$), and the same holds at V2. This advantage depends on the evaluation resolution: in the 5-seed model set of the resolution study (gap $+0.030$ at 224 px), it vanishes when the models are evaluated at their 32 px training resolution rho = -0.001, 95% CI $[-0.011, 0.009]$; arXiv:2608.12408). At LOC, BP, PC and STDP exceed the untrained baseline, FA is borderline, and the trained rules do not differ from each other. At IT, no two conditions can be distinguished at the low reliability of the data (leave-one-subject-out lower bound 0.021). FA has the lowest alignment at V1. At V1, an untrained network thus matches BP at the training resolution and exceeds it at 224 px; learning-rule differences are resolvable only at an intermediate area.

papers.title: Exact solution of two-dimensional Palatini Gauss-Bonnet theory on a strip
papers.abstract: We analyze the two-dimensional Palatini Gauss-Bonnet theory on an infinite strip (product of a finite interval with the infinite line, corresponding to ``time"). The theory has only boundary degrees of freedom. Its phase space is the cotangent bundle to the group manifold of $SL(2,\mathbf{R})$, subject to a (first-class) constraint quadratic in the momenta. With the simplest choice of boundary Hamiltonian, namely $H = 0$, the theory is shown to describe geodesics on the group manifold of $SL(2,\mathbf{R})$, with a ``mass" determined by the Palatini Gauss-Bonnet coupling constant. Other choices of boundary Hamiltonians compatible with gauge invariance are also possible. The symmetry group contains (left and right) group translations on $SL(2,\mathbf{R})$. These are ``boundary symmetries" from the bulk point of view, one copy acting on one end of the interval, the other copy acting on the other end. Comments on the quantum theory are also given.

papers.title: A Geometric Framework for Conditional Stability in Overdetermined Elliptic Problems
papers.abstract: We present a geometric framework for studying stability and symmetry in overdetermined elliptic boundary value problems. The approach is based on a normal radial parametrization of domains with respect to a strictly convex core $C$. We establish unconditional qualitative stability for second and fourth-order problems (Serrin and Bennett--Dalmasso). We then derive conditional quantitative stability estimates assuming a residual estimate for the tangential component. The method does not rely on moving planes or the maximum principle. The quantitative results are conditional upon a sufficient analytical assumption that we carefully formulate, including a control of the tangential gradient; we verify this assumption in two model cases. The quantitative results are stated and proved in the model case $C=\{0\}$; the general strictly convex core is discussed in Remark and left for future work.

papers.title: Blown-up singular Riemannian foliations
papers.abstract: We study the effect of projective blow-ups on the leaf closures and basic cohomology of singular Riemannian foliations. For a foliation with smooth Molino sheaf on a compact manifold, we show that the Molino sheaf of the blow-up is the inverse image of the original sheaf under blow-down. In particular, desingularization preserves the Killing property and the structural Lie algebra. We obtain a closedness criterion in terms of the Euler characteristics of the ambient manifold and the blow-up centers, assuming finite fundamental group and singular strata of codimension at least three. For singular Killing foliations on compact manifolds, we approximate the space of leaf closures in Gromov--Hausdorff distance by Riemannian orbifolds whose dimension equals the codimension of the foliation. Finally, relative basic cohomology gives a long exact sequence relating the original foliation, its blow-up, and their restrictions to the center and the exceptional divisor.

papers.title: Generalized Boltzmann-Gibbs Distributions and the Electronic Partition Function Paradox
papers.abstract: The maximization of the nonadditive entropic functional $S_{q}(p)=k\sum_{i}p_{i}\ln_{q}(1/p_{i})$, $q\in(0,1)$, under a linear mean-energy constraint, i.e., the best-behaved case from Dognini and Tsallis (2026), is used to derive generalizations of the Boltzmann-Gibbs distribution for physical systems whose description requires a limiting process over the energy spectrum: the hydrogen atom in free space; an energy spectrum that uniformly approaches a continuous, unbounded limit with a common degeneracy; the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution of velocities; the harmonic oscillator; and the one-dimensional box. For the hydrogen atom with mean energy $U\in[0,e_{ion}]$, the limiting optimal distribution is a two-tier one, concentrated on the ground level and on the ionization threshold, with weights $1-U/e_{ion}$ and $U/e_{ion}$ for every $q\in(0,1)$, and the temperature rescaled by $\ln_{q}W$ is finite and given by $T_{q,s}=T_{ion}(U/e_{ion})^{1-q}$, with $T_{ion}=e_{ion}/kq$. This circumvents the Electronic Partition Function Paradox and yields a family of well-defined thermodynamic behaviors.

papers.title: SURFing to the Fundamental Limit of Jet Tagging
papers.abstract: Beyond the practical goal of improving search and measurement sensitivity through better jet tagging algorithms, there is a deeper question: what are their upper performance limits? Generative surrogate models with learned likelihood functions offer a new approach to this problem, provided the surrogate correctly captures the underlying data distribution. In this work, we introduce the SUrrogate ReFerence (SURF) method, a new approach to validating generative models. This framework enables exact Neyman-Pearson tests by training the target model on samples from another tractable surrogate, which is itself trained on real data. We argue that the EPiC-FM generative model is a valid surrogate reference for JetClass jets and apply SURF to show that modern jet taggers may already be operating close to the true statistical limit. By contrast, we find that autoregressive GPT models unphysically exaggerate top vs. QCD separation power encoded in the surrogate reference, implying that they are giving a misleading picture of the fundamental limit.

papers.title: On a tamely ramified local relative Langlands conjecture via categorical representations
papers.abstract: Let $G$ be a complex reductive group. For a smooth affine spherical $G$-variety $X$ such that the stabilizer of a point in the $B$-orbit under the $B$-action be connected, assume that the unramified relative local Langlands conjecture of Ben-Zvi-Sakellaridis-Venkatesh (BZSV) for $X$ holds. We establish a spectral description of a full subcategory of Iwahori equivariant coherent D-modules on $LX$ in terms of the relative Langlands dual of $X$, confirming a tamely ramified local relative Langlands conjecture proposed by Devalapurkar.

papers.title: Learning Greens Operators through Hierarchical Neural Networks Inspired by the Fast Multipole Method
papers.abstract: The Fast Multipole Method (FMM) is an efficient numerical algorithm for computation of long-ranged forces in $N$-body problems within gravitational and electrostatic fields. This method utilizes multipole expansions of the Green's function inherent to the underlying dynamical systems. Despite its widespread application in physics and engineering, the integration of FMM with modern machine learning architectures remains underexplored. In this work, we propose a novel neural network architecture, the Neural FMM, that integrates the information flow of the FMM into a hierarchical machine learning framework for learning the Green's operator of an Elliptic PDE. Our Neural FMM architecture leverages a hierarchical computation flow of the FMM method to split up the local and far-field interactions and efficiently learn their respective representations.

papers.title: Differentiable-by-design Nonlinear Optimization for Model Predictive Control
papers.abstract: Nonlinear optimization-based control policies, such as those arising in nonlinear Model Predictive Control, have seen remarkable success in recent years. These policies require solving computationally demanding nonlinear optimization programs online at each time-step. The resulting solution map, viewed as a function of the measured state of the system and design parameters, may not be differentiable, which poses significant challenges if the control policy is embedded in a gradient-based policy optimization scheme. We propose a principled way to regularize the nonlinear optimization problem around the nominal solution, obtaining a surrogate derivative even if the solution map of the original problem is not differentiable. The surrogate problem is differentiable by design and its solution coincides with the solution of the unregularized problem. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in a free-final-time optimal control problem and a receding-horizon nonlinear MPC example.

papers.title: Asymptotic analysis on narrow tubes: narrow escape problems and diffusion processes
papers.abstract: This paper investigates a diffusion process in a narrow tubular domain with reflecting boundary conditions, where the geometry serves as a singular perturbation of an underlying graph in $\mathbb{R}^2$ or $\mathbb{R}^3$. The construction incorporates distinct scaling regimes in the neighborhoods of the graph's vertices and edges. We show that, in the limit, the projected process converges weakly to a diffusion process on the graph, with gluing conditions at the vertices that depend on the relative scales of the neighborhoods. Our analysis relies on a detailed understanding of the narrow escape problem in domains with bottlenecks. In particular, we rigorously derive the asymptotic behavior of the expected escape time, establish the asymptotic exponential distribution of escape times and obtain exit place estimates, results that may be of independent interest.

papers.title: Say It Another Way: Auditing LLMs with a User-Grounded Automated Paraphrasing Framework
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are highly sensitive to subtle changes in prompt phrasing, posing challenges for reliable auditing. Prior methods often apply unconstrained prompt paraphrasing, which risk missing linguistic and demographic factors that shape authentic user interactions. We introduce AUGMENT (Automated User-Grounded Modeling and Evaluation of Natural Language Transformations), a framework for generating controlled paraphrases, grounded in user behaviors. AUGMENT leverages linguistically informed rules and enforces quality through checks on instruction adherence, semantic similarity, and realism, ensuring paraphrases are both reliable and meaningful for auditing. Through case studies on the BBQ and MMLU datasets, we show that controlled paraphrases uncover systematic weaknesses that remain obscured under unconstrained variation. These results highlight the value of the AUGMENT framework for reliable auditing.

papers.title: Relativistic Navier-Stokes description of the quark-gluon plasma radial flow
papers.abstract: Using relativistic Navier-Stokes in the well-posed Bemfica-Disconzi-Noronha-Kovtun (BDNK) formulation, with a QCD equation of state and transport coefficients, we perform simulations that describe the radial flow in central Pb-Pb collisions measured at the LHC, providing a proof of principle for its viability in heavy-ion phenomenology. We identify causal frames that retain the Landau-frame interpretation, and verify frame robustness. Müller-Israel-Stewart simulations with identical input show large second-order effects, exceeding the frame dependence of relativistic Navier-Stokes, as well as causality violations.

papers.title: Ranking Statistical Experiments via the Linear Convex Order and the Lorenz Zonoid: Economic Applications
papers.abstract: This paper introduces a novel ranking of statistical experiments, the linear-Blackwell (LB) order, which can equivalently be characterized by (i) the dispersion of the induced posterior and likelihood ratios in the sense of the linear convex order, (ii) the size of the Lorenz zonoid (the set of statewise expectation profiles), or (iii) the variability of the posterior mean. We show that the LB order provides a necessary and sufficient criterion for comparing experiments uniformly across decision problems with quasi-concave payoffs and principal-agent problems with separable payoffs.

papers.title: NS-Gym: A Comprehensive and Open-Source Simulation Framework for Non-Stationary Markov Decision Processes
papers.abstract: Many real-world applications require decision-making where the environmental dynamics evolve over time. These non-stationary environments pose significant challenges to traditional decision-making models, which typically assume stationary dynamics. Non-stationary Markov decision processes (NS-MDPs) offer a framework to model and solve decision problems under such changing conditions. However, there are no standardized simulation frameworks for NS-MDPs, as opposed to widely popular frameworks for stationary problems. We present NS-Gym, the first simulation toolkit designed explicitly for NS-MDPs, integrated within the popular Gymnasium framework. In NS-Gym, we segregate the evolution of the environmental parameters that characterize non-stationarity from the agent's decision-making module, allowing for modular and flexible adaptations to dynamic environments. We review prior work in this domain and present a toolkit encapsulating key problem characteristics and types in NS-MDPs. This toolkit is the first effort to develop a set of standardized interfaces and benchmark problems to enable consistent and reproducible evaluation of algorithms under non-stationary conditions. We also benchmark several algorithmic approaches from prior work on NS-MDPs using NS-Gym. We envision that NS-Gym will enable researchers to study decision-making under non-stationarity by providing standardized interfaces, simulation frameworks, and benchmark problems. Project documentation, webpage, and code can be found at https://nsgym.io and https://github.com/scope-lab-vu/ns_gym

papers.title: Cohomological VC-density: Bounds and Applications
papers.abstract: The concept of Vapnik-Chervonenkis (VC) density is pivotal across various mathematical fields, including discrete geometry, probability theory and model theory. In this paper, we introduce a topological generalization of VC-density. Let $Y$ be a topological space and $\mathcal{X}$ a family of closed subspaces of $Y$. For each $p \geq 0$, we define a number, $\mathrm{vcd}^{p}_{\mathcal{X}}$, which we refer to as the degree $p$ VC-density of the family $\mathcal{X}$. The classical notion of VC-density within this topological framework can be recovered by setting $p=0$. Our definition of degree $p$ VC-density extends to higher orders as well. For $p \geq 0$, $q \geq 1$, we define the degree $p$, order $q$ VC density $\mathrm{vcd}^{p,q}_{\mathcal{X}}$ of $\mathcal{X}$, which recovers Shelah's notion of higher order VC-density for $q$-dependent families when $p=0$. Our definition introduces a completely new notion when $p > 0$. We examine the properties of $\mathrm{vcd}_{\mathcal{X}}^p$ (as well as $\mathrm{vcd}^{p,q}_{\mathcal{X}}$) when the families $\mathcal{X}$ are definable in structures with some underlying topology (for instance, the Euclidean topology for o-minimal structures over $\mathbb{R}$, the analytic topology over $\mathbb{C}$, or the étale site for schemes over arbitrary algebraically closed fields). Our main result establishes that in any model of these theories \[ \mathrm{vcd}_{\mathcal{X}}^p \leq (p+1) \dim X, \] and more generally for any $q \geq 1$ \[ \mathrm{vcd}^{p,q}_{\mathcal{X}} \leq (p+q) \dim X. \] We give examples to show that our bounds are optimal. We also present combinatorial applications of our higher-degree VC-density bounds, deriving higher degree topological analogs of well-known results such as the existence of $\varepsilon$-nets and the fractional Helly theorem.

papers.title: On completed homology and a conjecture of Venkatesh
papers.abstract: Let $F$ be a CM field and $Π$ a regular algebraic cuspidal cohomological representation of $\mathbf{G}=\operatorname{PGL}_2/F$. A conjecture of Venkatesh describes the structure of the contribution of $Π$ to the homology of the locally symmetric spaces associated to $\mathbf{G}$. We investigate this conjecture in the setting of $p$-adic homology with $p$ a totally split prime. Along the way, we elaborate on the relations between Venkatesh's conjecture and completed homology, the Taylor-Wiles method and the $p$-adic local Langlands correspondence. Our main result is a `big $R=T$' theorem in characteristic 0, from which we deduce a variant of the $p$-adic realisation of Venkatesh's conjecture, conditional on various natural conjectures and technical assumptions.

papers.title: High-Dimensional Tail Index Regression
papers.abstract: Motivated by the empirical observation of power-law distributions in the credits (e.g., ``likes'') of viral posts on social media, we introduce a high-dimensional tail index regression model and propose methods for estimation and inference of its parameters. First, we propose a regularized estimator, establish its consistency, and derive its convergence rate. Second, we construct a debiased version of the regularized estimator to facilitate inference and prove its asymptotic normality. Monte Carlo simulation studies corroborate our theoretical findings. We apply these methods (1) to the text analysis of viral posts on X (formerly Twitter) and (2) to the analysis of abnormally high health expenditures.

papers.title: Nanorobot queue: Cooperative treatment of cancer based on team member communication and image processing
papers.abstract: Although nanorobots have been used as clinical prescriptions for work such as gastroscopy, and even photoacoustic tomography technology has been proposed to control nanorobots to deliver drugs at designated delivery points in real time, and there are cases of eliminating "superbacteria" in blood through nanorobots, most technologies are immature, either with low efficiency or low accuracy, Either it can not be mass produced, so the most effective way to treat cancer diseases at this stage is through chemotherapy and radiotherapy. Patients are suffering and can not be cured. Therefore, this paper proposes an ideal model of a treatment method that can completely cure cancer, a cooperative treatment method based on nano robot queue through team member communication and computer vision image classification (target detection).

papers.title: DynSurvX: Time-Resolved Explanations for Dynamic Survival Predictions
papers.abstract: Recent survival models integrating longitudinal data achieve strong predictive performance, but their predictions are often difficult to interpret, limiting their clinical use. We propose DynSurvX, a model-agnostic explainability framework for dynamic survival prediction with mixed static and longitudinal covariates. Based on Shapley values, DynSurvX introduces a hierarchical two-phase strategy that first identifies influential longitudinal features and then adaptively refines their temporal importance, enabling fine-grained explanations while reducing computational cost. The framework provides time-resolved explanations that evolve as new patient data become available. Experiments on simulated and two clinical datasets show varying agreement with theoretical importance across prediction models, with closer agreement for better-performing models, alongside clinically interpretable insights in real-world settings. It remains robust across prediction settings and reduces computation time by 41--80\% relative to the temporal explanation baseline, making dynamic explanations practical.

papers.title: Astrophysical Constraints for Bosonic Dark Matter in and Around Quark Stars
papers.abstract: We investigate the structure, stability, and mass-radius relations of compact stars composed of quark matter within the non-ideal MIT Bag Model mixed with self-interacting bosonic dark matter with a $ϕ^n$ self-interaction potential. By solving the coupled two-fluid Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equations for boson masses between 200 MeV and 1 GeV and self-interaction strengths with $n=4$ and $n=40$, we show that strong self-interactions and higher boson masses enhance the stability of compact star configurations at high central pressures, though they reduce maximum overall masses. Ultra-compact solutions with $C \ge 1/3$ capable of mimicking black holes are significantly restricted compared to hadronic models, emerging only for strong self-interactions and dark matter fractions exceeding 90\%. Depending on the parameters, the compact stars form either extended dark matter halos or compact cores: stronger self-interactions and higher boson masses suppress the radial extension to favor compact cores of dark matter. Matching our models against observational constraints highlights PSR J1614$-$2230 and XTE J1814$-$338 as potential window of opportunity for dark matter detection. Notably, XTE J1814$-$338 could confirm a dark sector, given its requirement for light boson masses ($m_b \approx 200\text{--}300\text{ MeV}$) and strongly DM-dominated configurations.

papers.title: Lifting asymptotic symmetries from metric to tetrad formulation
papers.abstract: Metric solution spaces defined by gauge and boundary conditions are associated with a residual symmetry algebra, consisting of the diffeomorphism generators whose action preserves these conditions. Describing a metric solution space in terms of tetrad variables adds a local Lorentz freedom. When part of this freedom is fixed by additional tetrad gauge and boundary conditions, metric residual symmetries must be supplemented by compensating Lorentz transformations. If a residual Lorentz freedom remains, there is an ambiguity in these compensating transformations. The most direct choices generally fail to realize the metric residual symmetry algebra as a subalgebra of the tetrad one, because of a field-dependent cocycle. We show that a reference tetrad, that is a section of the tetrad solution space seen as a principal bundle over the metric one, always provides a lift free of this cocycle, so that the tetrad residual symmetry algebra is the semi-direct sum of the metric one and the ideal of field-dependent residual Lorentz transformations. The construction is independent of the gauge conditions, of the residual group, of the first-order Lagrangian, and reduces to the Kosmann lift on metric isometry generators. We illustrate it on a Weyl BMS-type solution space with time-dependent boundary metric, described in tetrad variables with a residual U(1) Lorentz freedom, for which the cocycle of a naive lift is computed and then explicitly removed.

papers.title: Two-Dimensional Kowalevski Top Problem as the Genus Two Full Jacobi Inversion Problem -Formulation Using Kolossoff Variables-
papers.abstract: For the Kowalevski top, we introduce another variable in addition to time variable, and formulate as the two-dimensional model. In this paper, since the results for the genus two full Jacobi inversion problem for the two variables Kowalevski top are already known, we utilize these results in reverse, introducing Kolossoff variables, to derive a more transparent formulation of the genus two full Jacobi inversion problem. Since there are two implicit equations of motion using Kowalevski variables, we derived two explicit equations of motion using Kolossoff variables, which is different from the Kolossoff method to derive only one explicit equation and to use Hamiltonian-Jacobi theory.

papers.title: HoloGene: Learning to Lift Sliced Spatial Transcriptomics to Holistic 3D Gene Fields
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) provides spatially resolved gene expression measurements, but most 3D ST datasets are acquired as independently processed 2D sections. Computational approaches span slice registration and integration, explicit or generative interpolation, and coordinate-field modeling. Within the last family, implicit neural representations (INRs) offer a continuous, coordinate-queryable parameterization, but standard isotropic coordinate encodings do not explicitly reflect that serial-section measurements are dense in-plane and sparse along the axial direction. We present HoloGene, an anisotropic conditional INR framework for estimating continuous 3D gene-expression fields from pre-registered ST sections. Its central contribution is an acquisition-aware factorization that couples dense in-plane synthesis with sparse axial evolution using established GAE, FiLM, pseudo-label supervision, and CORAL components. HoloGene compresses high-dimensional expression profiles into a graph-autoencoder latent manifold, uses pseudo-label-derived signature conditioning to provide coarse intra-section context, and applies depth-dependent FiLM modulation to model axial variation. A signature-stratified correlation-alignment regularizer encourages cross-slice covariance alignment in latent features. Using held-out measured sections as cross-sectional references, HoloGene improves reconstruction accuracy and biological preservation metrics compared with general-purpose INRs and adapted spatial-transcriptomics baselines. These results support anisotropic conditional modeling as a practical strategy for estimating 3D expression fields from discontinuous ST sections. Code is available at https://github.com/Szym29/HoloGene.

papers.title: Topological Splitting of Sondheimer Oscillations in Thin-Film Weyl Semimetals
papers.abstract: We discuss topological effects on Sondheimer oscillations in the magnetoresistance of thin-film Weyl semimetals. The Sondheimer oscillations are periodic in magnetic field and originate from the commensurability between the film thickness and the cyclotron-orbit pitch. Using Boltzmann transport theory, we investigate the effects of Berry curvature and orbital magnetic moment on the oscillations. We find that the Sondheimer oscillations split into two branches with different frequencies and that each branch becomes chirped because its frequency depends on magnetic field. These features originate from the orbital-Zeeman-induced deformation of the Fermi surface. The same mechanism also applies to Dirac semimetals.

papers.title: D/H and 12C/13C ratios of benzonitrile and indene in TMC-1 support bottom-up formation of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon-like molecules
papers.abstract: Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) have recently been detected in cold dark clouds through their rotational spectra, but it is currently a matter of debate whether they form through a bottom-up process from small hydrocarbons or through a top-down scenario involving the fragmentation of large PAHs inherited from a previous evolutionary stage of diffuse cloud. Isotopic ratios can shed light on the origin of PAHs in cold dark clouds. Large aromatic molecules observed in the infrared are enriched in deuterium and may also be enriched in 13C because they likely formed in the ejecta of evolved stars. We synthesized indene deuterated at the aliphatic position in the laboratory and measured its rotational spectrum, together with those of the nine 13C singly substituted isotopomers of indene. We used the measured spectra of the D and 13C isotopic species of indene, together with previously measured spectra of D and 13C isotopic benzonitrile, to search for these species in the cold dark cloud TMC-1 using QUIJOTE data obtained with the Yebes 40m telescope. We used a line stack method to tentatively detect deuterated benzonitrile and detect 13C-substituted benzonitrile, but find no evidence of either the D or 13C isotopic species of indene. We derive an aromatic D/H ratio of 0.53 % from benzonitrile, an aliphatic D/H ratio <3.3 % from indene, and 12C/13C ratios of 126 and >55 for benzonitrile and indene, respectively. These values are consistent with isotopic ratios derived for other molecules in TMC-1 and show no enrichment in either D or 13C that could be ascribed to inheritance from large PAHs in a top-down scenario; a bottom-up scenario is therefore the most likely.

papers.title: Revisiting Index Performance under High Cache-Miss Penalties
papers.abstract: Modern data-intensive applications often query very large datasets, making index performance critical. Recent index structures exploit the fine-grained access capabilities of emerging storage devices such as DCPMM and CXL. However, existing benchmarks typically evaluate indexes in isolation using saturated, closed-loop workloads that emphasize maximum throughput. Such workloads favor highly concurrent designs while overlooking the application work that follows an index lookup and competes for cache, memory bandwidth, and CPU resources. We present AuxBench - a microbenchmark that evaluates indexes as auxiliary access paths within larger application workloads. Using AuxBench, we evaluate four byte-addressable indexes under controlled post-lookup memory activity, concurrency, and request arrival patterns. Our experiments show that post-lookup memory activity can change the relative performance of competing indexes, that concurrency-oriented designs may lose their advantages when substantial application work is introduced, and that time-varying request arrivals can produce severe tail latency near saturation. These findings demonstrate why index-only benchmarks may not adequately predict performance in larger application workloads

papers.title: Forests of Omnitrees: Analysis and Applications to Anisotropic Space--Time Finite Elements
papers.abstract: We prove output-optimal work bounds for omnitree forests, which bisect cells along selected axes. A canonical descriptor characterizes representable partitions independently of split order. Complete one-level cycles, including coarsening, face balance and selected coarse meshes, take sequential work proportional to stored input and output at fixed dimension and key width, with polynomial depth dependence even for unbalanced input. From balanced input, refinement-only balance stays within each request's coordinate slab; this bound is attained. Polynomial trace equations characterize conforming high-order spaces across crossed face partitions. Reconstruction moments bound interpolation errors and capture the logarithmic loss that bilinear nodal interpolation can suffer on balanced meshes. Elements of degree up to four resolve moving heat layers on unstructured 4D space-time and 5D space-time-parameter meshes. Multigrid uses the generated hierarchies.

papers.title: Primal--Dual Kullback--Leibler Mirror-Prox for Dynamic Mean Field Games
papers.abstract: We compute finite-horizon dynamic mean field equilibria using a primal--dual Kullback--Leibler Mirror-Prox algorithm. Each iteration updates occupation measures by exponential tilting and computes the dual correction by solving a linear PDE, without solving a nonlinear Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman equation or a best-response control problem. Under assumptions and Lasry--Lions monotonicity, we prove an $O(K^{-1})$ ergodic Minty bound after $K$ iterations and an $O(K^{-1/2})$ approximate-equilibrium bound for the corrected average. We obtain convergence rates for the population flow under strong monotonicity, and for smooth diffusions with uniformly convex control costs under ordinary monotonicity. We also prove convergence of continuous-time Markov chain approximations to diffusion equilibria and, under additional smoothness and convexity assumptions, bound the error in terms of the spatial mesh size and the number of iterations. Galerkin approximations preserve the $O(K^{-1})$ estimates under suitable bounds on the correction errors. Numerical experiments illustrate the method and its convergence.

papers.title: Super-Eddington Accretion onto Compact Objects: Theory Meets Observation
papers.abstract: We review candidate super-Eddington populations together with semi-analytic models and radiation magnetohydrodynamic simulations, with the following conclusions: $\bullet$ Likely super-Eddington sources over a range of black hole mass show similar properties, including outflow on a range of scales, hard X-ray weakness, decreased emission from jets, and suppressed optical/UV variability. $\bullet$ Theoretical treatment of super-Eddington accretion predicts similar behavior across a range of methods and initial conditions, although interesting differences remain, particularly in the importance of magnetic fields. Numerical simulations produce a puffed-up inner disk with a funnel that grows narrower at higher mass accretion rate. Radiative efficiency declines with accretion rate in thermal-pressure--supported disks. $\bullet$ Ubiquitous outflow is likely an important ingredient in galaxy feedback at high Eddington ratios, as wind mechanical power increases with accretion rate and can rival jet power. Wind kinetic power depends far less on uncertain black hole spin and magnetic fields. $\bullet$ Observational classes of objects can be sorted in a two-dimensional parameter space of Eddington ratio and orientation. Observations down the funnel observe rapid X-ray variability, while observations through the wind will see suppressed X-ray emission. At the highest Eddington ratios, we envision a regime where the photosphere extends to $r > 10^6 \, r_g$, and the observer sees only thermalized emission covering most of the sky, speculatively corresponding to super-soft sources and Little Red Dots.

papers.title: VisHead-Spec: Head-Routed Visual Attention for Multimodal Speculative Decoding
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates vision-language models(VLMs) while preserving the target model's outputs, but its speedup diminishes under high concurrency serving as the system becomes more compute bounded as the batch size increases. This problem is pronounced for multimodal speculative decoding as the long range of the image tokens in the prompt can significantly increase the computational cost during draft token prediction. The block-diffusion drafters (e.g. DFlash, DSpark) can effectively speed up the draft model efficiency by predicting multiple draft tokens in one forward pass, but their speedup for VLMs under high concurrency is still modest (<9%). In order to understand this gap, we examine the information flow between different modalities from target model to draft model and identify the sparsity pattern of visual attention between the target and draft models: only small set of key-value heads in the draft model need direct visual feature attention in the context and only visual features from top level layers in the target model need to be attended in the context. We therefore propose VisHead-Spec, which selects a small, fixed set of key-value (KV) heads to attend to all image features from top level layers in the target model and restricts the remaining heads to text features. On Qwen3-VL-8B and MMSpec, VisHead-Spec-8 lets 8 of the drafter's 40 KV heads read the image while keeping accepted length within 0.3% of the block-diffusion draft model baseline (i.e. DSpark). At batch size 64, its throughput gain over autoregressive decoding increases to 16.0%, compared with 9.5% for DSpark; at batch size 1, its speedup remains comparable to DSpark.

papers.title: Quantum-Classical Separation in Probability Distribution Transport via Nonlocal Games
papers.abstract: In many-body physics and generative artificial intelligence, locality provides a natural notion of phase equivalence: two quantum states or classical probability distributions are regarded as in the same phase when local dynamics can reversibly transform one into the other. This raises a fundamental question: can local quantum dynamics transport classical probability distributions in ways that local classical dynamics cannot? We establish a quantum-classical separation in distribution transport: two classical distributions can be connected exactly and reversibly by a constant-depth local quantum circuit, whereas classical stochastic transport requires a substantially larger spatial range. We demonstrate this separation explicitly on a one-dimensional chain and develop a general construction principle on graphs, based on nonlocal games. Moreover, the source distribution can itself be generated by a simple local classical process, establishing a quantum advantage in distribution generation as well. Our results reveal a fundamental distinction between classical and quantum local reversibility, even when both the initial and final states are entirely classical.

papers.title: Three Dimensional Structure of Jovian Polar Cyclones Revealed by Juno Microwave Radiometer
papers.abstract: Jupiter's circumpolar cyclones (CPCs) represent one of the most extreme dynamical regimes of the Solar System, where rotation, stratification, and convection interact to organize a stable polygonal cyclone lattice at each pole. Yet the depth and vertical structure of these cyclones remain unresolved. Here, using Juno Microwave Radiometer observations acquired between May 2023 and May 2024, we retrieve the 3-D thermal/compositional structure of Jupiter's northern CPCs at depths beyond those detectable by Earth-based telescopes and spacecraft that have ever visited. The eight CPCs, appearing with enhanced microwave brightness, show as modest ammonia depletion near the water lifting-condensation level ($\sim$5 bar) and/or, equivalently, warm-core structures analogous to terrestrial tropical cyclones. Five of them show substantially stronger and deeper anomalies than the remaining three, with approximately twice the inferred ammonia depletion and localized heating. In contrast, the central polar cyclone exhibits little microwave brightness contrast relative to its surroundings, despite its substantially cloudier and visually distinct appearance in visible and infrared observations. Previous dynamical models have treated the CPCs and the central polar cyclone as dynamically similar structures arising from the self-organization of turbulent flows. The new observations, however, suggest that the CPCs and the central polar cyclone may have distinct origins and operate under different dynamical regimes.

papers.title: Simple Models of Thermal Order in $2+1$ Dimensions
papers.abstract: Heating need not destroy order. We show that it persists to arbitrarily high temperatures in simple quantum field theories in $2+1$ spacetime dimensions. In a $\mathbb Z_2\times\mathbb Z_2$ model of two real scalar fields, a sufficiently negative mixed quartic coupling drives one field to condense, spontaneously breaking its $\mathbb Z_2$ symmetry. When coupled to massless Dirac fermions through a Yukawa interaction, this condensate generates a fermion mass, thereby spontaneously breaking parity and time-reversal symmetries. We extend this construction to a $\mathbb Z_2\times O(n)$ scalar model, in which the Mermin-Wagner theorem precludes spontaneous breaking of the continuous $O(n)$ symmetry at finite temperatures. Nevertheless, for $n=2$, a Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless superfluid phase persists to arbitrarily high temperatures. In this phase, spatial correlations decay algebraically, with an exponent that approaches zero as the temperature increases. For $n\geq 3$, we uncover a further unexpected feature of these models: the characteristic size of ordered domains grows asymptotically with temperature, revealing an unusual enhancement of spatial correlations upon heating. We establish our results using a controlled high-temperature expansion, with selected findings corroborated by numerical functional renormalization group analysis. The simplicity of the field content in these models provides a promising starting point for exploring experimental realizations of persistent thermal order in thin-film materials.

papers.title: Structure Constants of Planar N=4 SYM at Any Coupling
papers.abstract: We recast a recent conjecture for structure constants in planar N=4 supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory in a separation-of-variables-inspired form suitable for non-perturbative analysis. All state-dependent information enters through the quantum spectral curve. As a showcase, we compute at finite coupling the three-point functions of two half-BPS operators and the spin-two member of the Konishi multiplet. Our results span weak to strong coupling, reproduce the known perturbative and string-theory limits, and are consistent with conformal-bootstrap bounds. We also obtain new six- and seven-loop perturbative coefficients and extract new strong-coupling data from high-precision numerical fits.

papers.title: Bias-Reduced and Parallel Heavy-Tailed Stochastic Convex Optimization in $\ell_p$ Geometries
papers.abstract: We consider the fundamental problem of parallel stochastic convex optimization (SCO), whose aim is to approximately minimize a convex objective when given the ability to query a moment-bounded stochastic gradient oracle multiple times in parallel per round. Whereas most previous results have focused on the variance-bounded Euclidean ($\ell_2$-norm) setting, meaning the objective is Lipschitz with respect to the $\ell_2$-norm over an $\ell_2$-bounded feasible set in $\mathbb{R}^d$, in this work we study parallel SCO in $\ell_p$ settings for $2 \le p < \infty$ under a heavy-tailed noise model. We begin by introducing a new class of $\ell_p$-optimal-distance-convergence (ODC$_p$) algorithms, drawing on prior stochastic bias-reduced techniques [ACJ+21], which combine with multilevel Monte Carlo methods to efficiently estimate the optimum of uniformly convex objectives. As a consequence of our ODC$_p$ algorithms, we first establish rates for projection-efficient $\ell_p$-Lipschitz optimization, composite convex minimization, and efficient $\ell_p$-proximal point estimation. Combining our ODC$_p$ algorithms with a new $\ell_p$-generalized Gaussian-based stochastic gradient estimator ($p$-GREG), we provide two efficient $\ell_p$ parallel algorithms, EpochDA and $\ell_p$-AC-SA, which achieve optimization error $ε> 0$ with at most $\tilde{O}(d^{\frac{p}{2p + 2}} ε^{-\frac{p}{p + 1}})$ query depth, improving upon the sequential heavy-tailed stochastic query depth of $O(ε^{-p})$ for $ε\leq \tilde{O}(d^{-1/(2p)})$. We also establish dimension-dependent lower bounds of $Ω\bigl(\min\{ε^{-p},d^{p/(3p-2)}\}\bigr)$ adaptive rounds for nonsmooth convex optimization over a subset of the unit $\ell_p$ ball. Our results improve upon the $Ω(\min\{ε^{-p},ε^{2/3}d^{1/3}\})$ bounds of [DG19], when adapted to the same feasible set.

papers.title: EmbedGym: Letting Coding Agents Develop and Debug Embedded Firmware Without Physical Hardware
papers.abstract: Modern coding agents perform well on general software benchmarks because they can run code and unit tests in a closed loop. Embedded firmware development, however, breaks this loop: a program that compiles can still fail on real hardware due to pin polarity, bus protocol, timing, or networking bugs that an agent at a text terminal cannot observe. Existing embedded coding agents either skip hardware execution, drive GPIO-only simulators with multi-second delays, or test on physical boards in a static environment. In this paper, we present EmbedGym, an interactive virtual hardware environment that lets coding agents develop and debug embedded firmware without physical hardware. EmbedGym uses instruction-level microcontroller unit (MCU) emulators to execute the same binary that would be flashed onto a physical board, connects them to 41 peripheral models, an analog circuit simulator, and virtual WiFi/Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) endpoints, and exposes an interface for agents to change sensor inputs, press buttons, and inspect hardware states. On top of it, we build EmbedGym-Bench, which consists of 598 tasks across 6 MCU-framework pairs graded by hidden timed test vectors, using a five-stage multi-agent workflow that synthesizes peripheral models and tasks from datasheets and driver libraries. We expose EmbedGym to a coding agent at three levels and evaluate eight models over more than 14K trajectories. Even when compilation succeeds 99.7% of the time, 19.9% of compiled firmwares fail at runtime (up to 73% on individual targets). In contrast, interactive hardware testing in EmbedGym increases pass rates across models by +4.9% to +14.7% (up to +31% on individual targets). Our results also show that an agent with EmbedGym outperforms prior embedded agent frameworks, and lightweight models with EmbedGym match frontier models without it at 30-70x lower cost.

papers.title: Can a World Model Predict a Deepfake Video? A Consistency Margin Prior for Deepfake Detection
papers.abstract: Deepfake detectors often perform well on the dataset they are trained on, but their performance drops when tested on videos from different datasets. In this paper, we study whether a predictive video model can provide a signal that generalizes better across datasets. Instead of relying only on generator-specific artifacts, as many existing detectors do, we use a model trained to predict natural video and measure the difference between what it predicts and what it observes in a video. Using V-JEPA 2.1, we keep the encoder frozen and adapt the predictor using rank-16 LoRA. We define the difference between the predictor output and the frozen encoder target as the prediction residual. We hypothesize that manipulated clips produce, on average, larger prediction residuals than authentic clips, and use this as our consistency-margin prior. We process these residuals using a lightweight Latent Consistency Head (LCH), which separates residual magnitude from direction for training and classification. To test whether the direction of the consistency margin affects cross-dataset generalization, we compare standard and reversed margin objectives while keeping the remaining training setup fixed. We match the two settings on FF++ validation performance before evaluating them on unseen data. The reversed-margin setting exhibits a larger cross dataset generalization gap on average, providing evidence that the direction of the consistency margin affects cross-dataset transfer. Our complete model adds only 8.25M trainable parameters, which is 2.47% of the total 334M parameters. Trained only on FF++, it achieves an AUC of 90.5 on Celeb-DFv2 and performs well across several other cross-dataset benchmarks. Our ablations show that separating residual magnitude from direction, reducing dataset-specific variation, and using a low-rank projection improve cross-dataset generalization in our experiments.

papers.title: Inventa: Decentralized Self-Improving Agents for Autonomous Scientific Discovery
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can generate research ideas and improve scientific discovery through iterative experimentation. However, increasing the number of agents or iterations does not automatically translate to producing more diverse or feasible ideas. Agents may converge on similar candidates, propagate unsupported claims through shared memory components and repeatedly apply search strategies that no longer yield any improvements. We introduce Inventa, a framework for automated scientific discovery that employs autonomous research units and verified shared knowledge. Each unit creates a lineage of candidate ideas using a mutator agent. A local orchestrator agent periodically adapts the mutator's harness. When progress stalls, the orchestrator agent replaces its model or restarts the idea evolution process. Verifiers evaluate each candidate idea and record verified improvements, useful components and constraint violations in a shared knowledge, the only channel between units. We evaluate Inventa on five benchmarks spanning the research cycle, covering retrieval (ScholarCatalyst), ideation (IdeaBench), proposal writing (IdeaScientist), and scientific law discovery (EurekaBench, SciLaws-Bench). It leads all five, achieving 73.6% on EurekaBench versus 56.2% for CORAL. On IdeaBench, it discovers 26.0 novel ideas per paper, compared with 18.6 for ResearchAgent, with 82% fewer model calls.

papers.title: High-resolution top-down nanopatterning of NbN thin films for superconducting metamaterials
papers.abstract: Periodic nanopatterning offers a route to tailoring vortex motion and the electromagnetic response of superconducting films, providing a basis for superconducting metamaterials. Here, we report a high-resolution top-down nanopatterning process for ultrathin epitaxial NbN films on sapphire substrates. Electron-beam lithography using hydrogen silsesquioxane (HSQ) and ZEP 530A resists was optimized through proximity-effect correction and adhesion-layer integration. Dense superconducting nanowire grids with pitches down to 70 nm were fabricated, alongside millimeter-square areas patterned with 100-nm-pitch hole arrays with high pattern fidelity. A thin Si capping layer was found to significantly improve HSQ adhesion on epitaxial NbN. The nanopatterns were successfully transferred into 5-nm-thick NbN films by reactive ion etching (RIE). Structural and dimensional characterization was performed using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), and atomic force microscopy (AFM), enabling cross-validation of nanoscale feature dimensions and etch quality. Electrical transport measurements reveal periodic resistance minima and switching-current oscillations at magnetic fields set by the hole-array pitch, consistent with enhanced vortex pinning when the vortex configuration matches the patterned lattice. Cryogenic THz time-domain spectroscopy further reveals a reduced superfluid density in the nanopatterned region relative to pristine NbN, while both regions have a spectroscopic superconducting transition near 14 K. These results establish a robust fabrication platform for superconducting nanopatterns targeting vortex pinning, metamaterials, and quantum-device applications.

papers.title: When Does Discrete Ricci Curvature Help? An Edge-Level Analysis of Curvature-Enhanced GCNs for PPI Prediction
papers.abstract: Curvature-enhanced graph convolutional networks (CGCN) incorporate Ollivier-Ricci curvature (ORC), grounded in optimal transport theory, into message passing, motivated by the claim that curvature-weighted edges alleviate "over-squashing" at structural bottlenecks. But does CGCN's improvement actually come from mitigating over-squashing? We investigate this on four real-world protein-protein interaction (PPI) datasets, comparing CGCN against a standard GCN at the level of individual edges rather than aggregate metrics alone. While CGCN improves aggregate AUC, AUPR, and F1 across all four datasets, this gain is concentrated almost entirely on low-degree edges, while performance on low-curvature (bottleneck) edges systematically degrades in three of four datasets, the opposite of what the over-squashing motivation predicts. Examining the learned edge-weight function directly, together with clustering-validity metrics, edge-distance ratios, and a layer-depth ablation across four depths, we find evidence for an alternative account: curvature-weighting sharpens the separation between clusters, which improves intra-cluster predictions at the cost of inter-cluster (bottleneck) ones. We test this account against topologically defined communities rather than the classification labels used elsewhere. Additionally, we offer practical guidance on when to prefer CGCN over standard GCN, depending on whether intra- or inter-cluster predictions matter most.

papers.title: Improved accuracy of the reference photon calibration standards in the network of gravitational-wave observatories during the O4 observing run
papers.abstract: The global network of gravitational wave observatories uses systems known as Photon Calibrators to provide absolute calibration via laser radiation pressure. Successive detector improvements are increasing sensitivity, enabling not only increase the detection rate but also detections with high signal to noise ratios. To optimally extract information from these detected signals, continual effort is directed at pushing the state of the art of the interferometer calibration accuracy. To improve the accuracy of the locally-maintained laser power standards for photon calibration, a new global calibration scheme was implemented by using transfer standards calibrated at both the National Institute of Standards and Tech- nology (NIST) in the US and the Physikalisch-Technische Bundesanstalt (PTB) in Germany during the recently completed fourth observing run. We report the results of a long-duration NIST-PTB bilateral comparison conducted over almost three years and the results of propagation of transfer standard calibrations to the reference power sensors maintained at each observatory.

papers.title: AR-WAM: efficient streaming world-action modeling for autonomous driving
papers.abstract: Autonomous driving requires anticipating how traffic will evolve while responding quickly to new observations. Video foundation models offer the first ability, but repeated history encoding and iterative video generation make them costly to use for driving. We present AR-WAM, an efficient streaming world-action model that combines autoregressive temporal modeling with single-pass future conditioning. Because its video backbone is causal, AR-WAM updates its visual context incrementally, reusing past computation and conditioning future prediction on observed motion. We further hypothesize that future features computed from recent observations can improve generalization in dynamic traffic without iterative video generation. AR-WAM therefore obtains these features in one forward pass and uses them to condition trajectory generation, and reinforcement learning then improves the policy through direct optimization of driving rewards. With a single front camera, AR-WAM achieves 91.5 PDMS after supervised training and 94.0 after reinforcement learning on NAVSIM-v1, outperforming the compared strong end-to-end world-action models. In a dynamic setting of continuous driving, supervised AR-WAM keeps its visual history across decisions and outperforms strong world-action baselines.

papers.title: The Hidden Cost of MoE Diffusion Decoding: Profiling and Fixing the Sampler
papers.abstract: Masked diffusion language models (dLLMs) decode by iteratively denoising a full canvas of tokens, so every forward pass runs a per-token sampling and stopping pipeline over the entire canvas-by-vocabulary logits tensor. We profile single-user decoding of a 26B-parameter diffusion Mixture-of-Experts model on a bandwidth-bound edge accelerator (NVIDIA GB10) and report a result that is easy to miss: after weight quantisation, this logits pipeline, not the expert GEMMs, is the single largest consumer of decode time. Unlike autoregressive decoding, where sampling touches one position's logits per committed token, diffusion decoding processes S times as many logit entries per output token, where S is the number of denoising steps. We show this pipeline is largely redundant or fusable and remove it in two lossless tiers: a bit-exact tier whose output is byte-identical to the reference decoder, and an accuracy-parity tier using a fused single-pass entropy kernel and Gumbel-max sampling. Combined with a W4A16 expert kernel, the full stack reaches 2.4-2.7 times end-to-end speedup over bf16 at unchanged benchmark accuracy on GSM8K, HumanEval, and MATH, on a single 273 GB/s device. We confirm the finding on a second, independently built diffusion MoE (LLaDA2.0-mini: pipeline 28.8% of decode, fused W4A16 3.3 times at accuracy parity) and show it disappears on a dense diffusion model (3.6%). The cost is specific to MoE diffusion, where quantisation makes the backbone cheap. Code and quantised weights are released.

papers.title: Translation surfaces with logarithmically growing systole
papers.abstract: We exhibit a sequence of translation surfaces $T_1, T_2,...$ with $T_g$ of genus $g$ and area $g$, such that the systole grows logarithmically with $g$. They are produced by starting with a fixed translation surface, taking covers with the same topology as those discovered by Brooks, and then adding handles by gluing along slits.

papers.title: Kernel Tuning for the HSIC-Based Global Sensitivity Analysis of High-Dimensional Models
papers.abstract: We consider global sensitivity analysis of models with high-dimensional input parameters using HSIC-based indices. The numerical estimation of these kernel-based indices is known to be challenging for such models. Without proper kernel tuning, the standard estimator for the HSIC can become unstable and break down. Focusing on models with independent parameters, we introduce a dimension-aware bandwidth formula and provide theoretical analysis justifying the proposed approach. In particular, we show that unless kernel bandwidth parameters explicitly scale with the input dimension, the corresponding sensitivity indices return uninformative rankings of parameter influence. Further, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed scaling strategy on linear and nonlinear test problems, including models with correlated inputs.

papers.title: Shortest-path percolation and structural robustness of quantum internet networks
papers.abstract: We study shortest-path percolation on spatial networks that model the quantum internet based on optical fibers. In this process, the removal of paths describes the consumption of the entangled links used for communication. We compare finite and unrestricted path-length bounds for networks whose average degree either increases with system size or remains approximately constant. We show that networks become more robust as the average degree increases, whereas networks with approximately constant average degree exhibit a data collapse for the fixed finite bounds considered. Using Monte Carlo sampling of the shortest-path-length distribution, we estimate an equivalent path cost, a finite bound that approximately reproduces the degradation of the network in the unrestricted case. For networks with fixed average degree, this cost grows approximately as the square root of the number of nodes. Increasing the bound beyond this value requires additional computation time without appreciably changing the percolation dynamics. As a complementary result, for Erdős-Rényi random networks, we find an empirical relation between the initial average degree and the approximately common crossing point of the percolation curves for different path-length bounds.

papers.title: Optimal Network Design under Node Failures
papers.abstract: Networks are frequently constructed before it is determined which nodes will persist. We address the design problem in scenarios where nodes fail independently, links are costly and must be established in advance, and the benefits to surviving nodes diminish with distance.
