That is, we will see that there is both "good news" and "bad news" when one studies the positivity preserving properties of Green's operators associated with higher order elliptic differential operators on smooth, closed Riemannian manifolds and the eigenproblem for higher order elliptic differential operators on smooth, closed Riemannian manifolds.

papers.title: ETH is Dead, Long Live SH
papers.abstract: Among the recent flood of AI-based mathematical breakthroughs (the "mathpocalypse"), perhaps the biggest bombshells in theoretical computer science were two disproofs of the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH), via slightly subexponential algorithms for the classic $k$-Satisfiability problems. After the initial shock, the community quickly began to wonder at the implications: how do the hundreds if not thousands of ETH-based lower bounds in the literature need to change? It turns out, not much -- if we are willing to change the exponents ever so slightly. While Impagliazzo and Paturi's 1999 Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH) is false, Stearns and Hunt's 1990 Satisfiability Hypothesis (SH) remains plausible. We prove that SH is equivalent to the recently proposed Weak ETH which rules out $O(2^{n^{1-\varepsilon}})$-time 3SAT algorithms for every constant $\varepsilon>0$, where $n$ is the number of variables. We show that SH (or Weak ETH) preserves the typical process for lower bounds: a polynomial-time reduction from a 3SAT formula of size $s$ (the number of variables plus clauses) to an instance of size $N\le s^{b+o(1)}$, for fixed blowup exponent $b>0$, rules out $O(2^{N^{1/b-\varepsilon}})$-time algorithms for every constant $\varepsilon>0$. By comparison, for an $N=O(s^b)$ blowup, ETH would have ruled out $2^{o(N^{1/b})}$-time algorithms. The framework also yields parameterized lower bounds ruling out a running time of $O(2^{k^{1/b-\varepsilon}})L^{O(1)}$ when the reduction produces an instance of length $L$ with parameter $k\le s^{b+o(1)}$. We also prove equivalence of the analogous counting hypotheses, #SH and Weak ETH, and that they rule out $O(2^{s^{1-\varepsilon}})$-time algorithms for #2SAT formulas of size $s$ for every constant $\varepsilon>0$.

papers.title: Malware Clustering in the Wild: Taxonomy, Challenges, and Evaluation Metrics
papers.abstract: As malware continues to grow in volume, diversity, and sophistication, clustering has emerged as a critical technique for analyzing large malware corpora. Clustering enables the discovery of structural relationships, behavioral patterns, and evolutionary trends, and is widely used to group unknown samples, infer malware family boundaries, and identify novel variants. However, existing research remains fragmented, employing a wide range of clustering techniques with no unified perspective that systematically organizes prior work or clearly identifies gaps in the literature. This survey addresses this gap by organizing previous malware clustering research into seven categories: centroid-based, hierarchical-based, density-based, distribution-based, mixed- type, fuzzy, and AI-driven approaches. In addition, this survey summarizes publicly available malware datasets commonly used in clustering research and examines the feature representations derived from these datasets. Our goal is to clarify the current landscape and outline promising avenues for future research on malware clustering, including how AI-driven methods may shape large-scale and reproducible analysis.

papers.title: Near-horizon BF bounds for the $t^+$ KK tower on extremal AdS$_5$ black holes
papers.abstract: We study the charged Breitenlohner--Freedman (BF) bound for all horizon harmonics of the type IIB $t^+$ Kaluza--Klein tower on extremal charged AdS$_5$ black holes with equal rotations. The scalar equation follows from maximal five-dimensional gauged supergravity at level zero and the linearized exceptional-field-theory equations at higher levels. For aligned charge and rotation, a quadratic form in charge and spin changes signature on the curve of supersymmetric (BPS) black holes, where every mode satisfies the bound. Above the curve, where $Ω_H>1$, every black hole has a violating mode, although no finite truncation in level or spin detects violation at every such black hole. Below the curve, where $Φ_H>1$, the BF-passing set is confined to a thin strip and controlled by charge and spin discreteness. At large radius and fixed rotation, a level-four mode with spin proportional to the radius violates the bound even where all U(2) singlets satisfy it. These results concern the near-horizon BF bound of one tower in two-derivative supergravity; full radial stability remains open.

papers.title: Cassette-Editor: Shared Timeline Semantics for Human and Agent Editing
papers.abstract: Video editing involves tedious manual manipulation across interconnected timeline tracks, motivating automated agents that offload routine work while keeping the project directly revisable by humans. Fixed operation catalogs limit expressiveness, while even a basic trim requires coordinated updates across later clips, attached titles, and transitions. We present Cassette-Editor, an agent harness that unifies manual user gestures and automated agent patches within a shared editing environment. The shared action language expresses the editor's manual content changes, and a common history records committed edits for undo and manual refinement. When the model selects an edit, a state executor automatically derives its downstream consequences, such as shifting later clips and attached titles after a trim, while a validation rulebook enforces structural invariants and returns localized diagnostics for automated repair. To keep the agent grounded as the project evolves, dynamic read operations map transcripts and shot descriptions onto the current timeline. Evaluated with GPT-6 Luna, the full harness passed the scored request checks in 92/93 trials across 31 authored requests on two interview documentaries, compared with 48/93 for an internal basic-tools baseline. In ablations, disabling the consequences derived by the executor reduced passed trials from 230/232 to 199/232 on edits with dependent timeline elements, while ablating rulebook validation and repair lowered passed trials from 46/48 to 10/48 on requests operating near structural validity boundaries. Evaluating the complete system on 50 TVSum videos further demonstrated greater agreement with human annotations than a general agent using the same model (F1 23.8 vs. 20.1).

papers.title: The Legendre potential and the gradient case of the differential Galois criterion for the Jacobian Conjecture
papers.abstract: Let $h\in\C[X_1,\dots,X_n]$ have constant nonzero Hessian determinant, let $h^{*}$ be its formal Legendre transform and $g=\vv{X,\grad h}-h$. The Nambu derivations of $\grad h$ satisfy $δ_i(g)=X_i$ and $δ^α(g)=(\partial^αh^{*})\circ\grad h$. Consequently, in the gradient case the differential Galois criterion of \cite{ACH19}, consisting of $n$ membership conditions, reduces to a single membership condition. Equivalently, $\grad h$ is a polynomial automorphism if and only if $g\in\C[\partial_1h,\dots,\partial_nh]$. Moreover, $\grad h$ is a polynomial automorphism if and only if $δ^α(g)=0$ for $|α|=(°h-1)^{n-1}+2$, and then the coefficients $δ^α(g)(x_0)/α!$ of $h^{*}$ at $\grad h(x_0)$ determine the inverse. If the Hessian determinant of $h$ is merely a nonzero polynomial, then $g$ is still a primitive element of $\C(X)$ over $\C(\partial_1h,\dots,\partial_nh)$. For the Nambu-tower criterion, doubling a Keller map yields no independent conditions. After an affine change of coordinates putting $\grad h$ in the normal form $X+H$, the formal Legendre transform is the sum of the formal Pascal difference series of $g$, and the termination of this series implies polynomial invertibility. In at most three variables the normal form of every gradient Keller map has strongly nilpotent Jacobian part and is therefore Pascal finite, by a theorem of de Bondt, and an explicit gradient automorphism in four variables has a normal form which is not Pascal finite. The five-variable counterexample of Meng and Yang shows that the properties used here do not imply the Hessian conjecture. The results do not settle the open cases $\JC_2$ and $\HC_4$.

papers.title: Critical measures and coefficient limits for non-Gaussian holomorphic chaos
papers.abstract: We study critical holomorphic multiplicative chaos with circular iid inputs of unit variance. Writing \(R=|X_1|\), the radially normalized boundary measures converge in probability to a finite measure with almost surely positive mass exactly when \(\mathbb{E}[R^2\log(2+R)]<\infty\); otherwise they converge to zero. Radial and Fourier--radial approximations have distinct sharp \(L^q\) convergence criteria at each \(0<q<1\); convergence at every such order holds for both families exactly when \(\mathbb{E}e^{sR}<\infty\) for every \(0<s<2\). In the positive-limit class, coefficient vectors multiplied by \((\log n)^{1/4}\) and their analytic windows converge stably to Gaussian mixtures determined by the same critical measure. A uniformly bounded input family gives uncountably many coefficient-limit laws inequivalent under nonzero deterministic complex rescaling. We distinguish these laws using exact weighted tails under \(\mathbb{E}I_0(2R)<\infty\), where \(I_0\) is the modified Bessel function, and negative mass moments. For \(\log\mathbb{P}(R>u)\sim-λu^α\), \(0<α<1\) and \(λ>0\), the normalization and Gaussian-mixture form persist, while every positive limit moment diverges; we determine the logarithmic tails. Finite limiting moments need not imply convergence of the original coefficient moments. In the positive-limit class, coefficient periodograms recover the critical measure and energy normalization gives Gaussian limits. Hardy nonmembership holds under finite variance alone; the positive-limit class has sharp weighted Bergman criteria for \(0<p\le2\) and boundary Sobolev threshold \(s=-1/2\).

papers.title: ASR-Protected Fusion and Reference-Anchored Policy Optimization for Joint ASR and Word-Level Speech Anti-Spoofing
papers.abstract: Existing anti-spoofing systems report either an utterance-level score or a time-based spoof interval: the former cannot show which words are spoofed, while the latter does not directly match the transcript and must be post-aligned with words, so alignment errors can lead to wrong word-level labels. Standard ASR model outputs only text; spoof information in the audio is lost after recognition and is not passed with the transcript. Yet changing only a few words can change the meaning of a sentence, leaving downstream systems to use incorrect text without knowing which words are spoofed. We therefore treat partial anti-spoofing as tagged ASR: the model transcribes speech and marks spoofed words at the same time, directly linking spoof labels to output words. We adopt the audio LLM and use ASR-Protected Subspace Gated Fusion (APSGF) to fuse spoof cues with ASR features. Spoof cues are added only outside an ASR-protected subspace, so they do not disturb recognition features. After cross-entropy training, we fine-tune the model with Reference-Anchored Policy Optimization (RAPO). Since the SFT policy is already concentrated, multiple samples from the same input tend to receive similar rewards, resulting in weak group-wise advantages. RAPO instead generates a single sample with low sampling randomness and anchors its advantage to the reward of a reference model. This allows the model to reinforce responses that outperform the reference while suppressing those that underperform it. Experiments on five datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in jointly detecting spoofed words and preserving ASR accuracy. The code is publicly available.

papers.title: Asymptotic analysis of Dirichlet problems in supercritically perforated domains via quantification by torsional rigidity
papers.abstract: We study the Dirichlet problem $-\mathrm{div}(A^{\varepsilon}\nabla u^{\varepsilon}) = f$ on varying open sets $D^{\varepsilon}$, with uniformly elliptic coefficients $A^{\varepsilon}$, in the regime where the solutions vanish in the limit for every source. For periodically perforated domains, this is the supercritical regime. We show that the torsional rigidity $T(D^{\varepsilon})$ is the natural normalization: up to a subsequence, $u^{\varepsilon}/T(D^{\varepsilon})$ converges weakly as measures to $kf$ for every continuous source $f$, where $k$ is a nonzero finite measure independent of $f$, which we call the effective measure. The key ingredient is an estimate comparing $u^{\varepsilon}$ with the product of $f$ and the torsion function, whose rate depends on the domains only through $T(D^{\varepsilon})$. We also show that this rate is optimal. No structural assumption on the perforation is needed, and the results hold for relaxed Dirichlet problems. Every nonzero finite measure arises as an effective measure, so the continuity of the source cannot be dropped in general. For rougher sources, we characterize the convergence by a condition on the domains alone, expressed through their torsion functions or, equivalently, their Poincaré constants. We also prove that the effective measure is local, satisfies optimal two-sided bounds and is monotone with respect to the coefficients, and we study the role of the antisymmetric parts of the coefficients.

papers.title: Rotation in the Lagoon Nebula with K2
papers.abstract: A low-mass star's rotation rate drives its magnetic field, and in the case of young stars, also affects accretion and planetary formation. Observations of the rotation rates of young stars help constrain models of star and planet formation. We present rotation rates from K2 observations of stars in the ~1-2 Myr Lagoon Nebula, one of the youngest clusters with space-based rotation rates available. From 414 light curves we obtain reliable rotation periods for 325 stars; 124 of them are disk-bearing and 201 are disk-free. This constitutes a significant increase in the collection of K2 rotation rates available for ~1-5 Myr stars. The overall distribution is broadly consistent with expectations, in that the slowest rotators are mid-K and both lower and higher masses are on average faster rotating. There is weak evidence that disked stars rotate more slowly. There are a few complex periodic variables, but they appear to be surprisingly high mass compared to prior known examples of this kind of object.

papers.title: On Maximum Clique and Maximum Consensus Formulations in Point Cloud Registration
papers.abstract: Maximum clique and maximum consensus are widely used formulations for robust point cloud registration. Maximum consensus seeks one transformation that aligns as many matches as possible, while maximum clique selects matches through pairwise distance tests. Maximum clique is often used as a substitute for or an approximation to maximum consensus, with empirical evidence suggesting a close relationship. However, how closely the two formulations agree is not fully understood. We study this relationship theoretically. We show that, at any fixed positive tolerance, a maximum clique can have arbitrarily large alignment error and be arbitrarily larger than a maximum consensus set. When rotation is fixed, we derive sharp error bounds and tests that exactly characterize maximum consensus for the translation subproblem. We also study group-$k$ consistency, which uses consistency of groups of $k$ matches, and determine the smallest group sizes that guarantee alignment error bounds independent of point cloud scale and geometry. These are $d+1$ for rotations and translations and $d+2$ when reflections are allowed, in dimensions $d\ge2$. Finally, our experiments on nearly 8,000 registration examples quantify the frequency of these limitations in practice and show how the derived bounds can be used to check whether a subset of matches can be aligned within a point tolerance.

papers.title: Realtime-Bench: Can Frontier Models Solve Real-time Interactive Problems?
papers.abstract: Real-time interaction requires agents to perceive evolving environments and act under temporal constraints, yet existing evaluations of real-time streaming models focus on conversational quality and streaming perception, leaving effective action under strict temporal constraints untested. We introduce Realtime-Bench, a suite of carefully curated dynamic tasks where delayed actions directly affect success. Under Wall Clock, where environments advance according to actual inference latency, the best success rate reaches only 44% and the best Pass^3 is only 36%, demonstrating that real-time interaction remains challenging. To separate serving latency from models' real-time streaming capability, we compare Wall Clock with Paused Clock, which removes inference delays as an idealized reference, and introduce Token Clock, which advances simulated time according to generated token counts, testing temporal awareness independently of physical serving speed. We find that temporal costs limit success in evolving environments and that higher reasoning effort has mixed effects under time pressure, reflecting a trade-off between decision quality and timely execution. Based on these results, we discuss future directions for improving real-time multimodal models, including adaptive reasoning with temporal awareness and continuous perception and action.

papers.title: Nambu's Dynamics, Strings and Gravitized Quantum Theory
papers.abstract: In this article we present a new view on string theory that is rooted in quantum foundations extended to the domain of quantum gravity in the form of gravitized quantum theory, in which the canonical probability measure captured by the Born rule of quantum theory, turns out to be dynamical and contextual. We claim that this gravitization of quantum theory is the essence of string theory. String theory, according to this view, originates in foundations of quantum theory and Nambu's dynamics, which features in the non-perturbative definition of string theory in terms of a T-duality covariant and non-commutative formulation, called the metastring. Nambu's dynamics and the associated cubic and hypercubic objects also appear as the natural language for exploring the new observables and phenomena implied by a dynamical Born rule, including triple and higher order quantum interference, that can be investigated in experiments involving massive quantum probes, and that are also needed for direct empirical tests of the Born rule, a cornerstone of quantum theory.

papers.title: DASH: A da Vinci Adapter for Serial-link and Humanoid Robots as an Accessible Platform for Surgical Robotics Research
papers.abstract: Robotic minimally invasive surgery offers well-documented clinical benefits, but the cost and infrastructure requirements of purpose-built platforms limit access in rural and lower-resourced facilities. Recent work has teleoperated general-purpose robots for laparoscopic tasks and in vivo procedures, but relied on handheld instruments coupled through passive linkages rather than native robotic actuation. Instead, we adapt da Vinci Classic and Xi instruments onto general-purpose robots that can integrate in clinical workflows. We present DASH, a da Vinci Adapter for Serial-link and Humanoid platforms, consisting of two types of adapters that require no modification to the instruments themselves. Each adapter is compatible with many robotic platform load capacities, engages the instrument's native latch, and wirelessly identifies inserted tools to load instrument-specific kinematics and coupling matrices. Teleoperated experiments demonstrate the efficacy of DASH and its benefits for enabling research access to surgical robotic platforms. DASH has been open sourced at https://github.com/sarawickenhiser/DASH_open_source.

papers.title: Revisiting damping of Alfvén waves in partially ionized plasmas
papers.abstract: We investigate the damping rate of Alfvén waves by means of the linear analysis of the two-fluid ten-moments system. To treat effects of viscosity in a wide frequency range, we take account of the time evolution of the traceless part of the pressure tensor. In addition, to treat effects of viscosity in a wide range of the ionization degree, we consider interactions between hydrogen atoms and between protons and hydrogen atoms in the equation of the traceless part of the pressure tensor. We find approximate analytical solutions to the dispersion relation for some limits. Our analysis in the low-frequency limit shows that the viscous damping dominates over the frictional damping in the high-beta plasma, which is independent of the ionization degree. Therefore, the viscosity of hydrogen gas significantly affects cosmic-ray propagation in a partially ionized high-beta plasma.

papers.title: When Terminal-Agent Training Stalls: Demystifying Data Generation and Verification Challenge
papers.abstract: Automated terminal-agent training relies on generated environments and verifiers to turn open-ended interaction into reward. Yet a runnable Docker image and executable test suite do not guarantee that the resulting reward is faithful, informative, or even attributable to agent behavior. We present a pipeline that generates containerized terminal tasks and their executable verifiers, and use it to demystify failure modes in task generation and live-environment evaluation. Our analysis separates four requirements that are often conflated: structural validity, verifier faithfulness, policy solvability, and infrastructure reliability. In a GRPO training of Qwen3.5-9B, it overfits on a relatively easy dataset within 20 steps. Conversely, in a controlled Qwen3.5-9B comparison, adding hard tasks lowers mean rollout pass@2 from 81.3% to 20.6%, restoring informative failures without changing the training configuration. We further identify near-duplicate task generation, incomplete anti-shortcut safeguards, Dockerfile failures, asynchronous pass@k bias, and concurrency-induced environment errors as distinct threats to measurement. These findings should motivate the community for a terminal agent specific evaluation harness that pairs structural checks and rollout-derived solvability with extensive verifier audits.

papers.title: Zong's problem on $2d$ half-spaces containing the unit ball
papers.abstract: We prove that the intersection of $2d$ half-spaces containing the Euclidean unit ball in $\mathbb{R}^d$ contains a point of norm at least $\sqrt{d}$. Equality in the radius bound characterizes the cube up to orthogonal transformations. The proof gives a lower bound for the average squared norm of the vertices, weighted by the Gaussian measures of their normal cones. This estimate follows from an inequality for the Gaussian measures of a simplicial cone and its projected facets, which in turn reduces to a linear estimate for the Gaussian centroid of a simplicial cone. We also discuss a quadratic extension of the problem and give a bound for it using an independent spectral argument. This bound implies that the intersection of any $m > d$ half-spaces containing the unit ball contains a point of norm at least $\sqrt{m}\,\ln\frac{m}{m-d}$.

papers.title: Hidden Rotational Dynamics from Crystal Geometry
papers.abstract: From hidden spin order to electronic loop currents and frustrated fluctuations, unconventional quantum matter reveals the rich patterns that electronic and magnetic degrees of freedom form across space and time. Recent advances in chiral phononics have extended this perspective to lattice vibrations, raising the question of whether the lattice itself can generate spatially organized rotational correlations. Here we show that crystal geometry provides an autonomous mechanism for generating equilibrium angular-momentum circulation and staggered antisymmetric displacement interactions, independently of coupling to electronic or magnetic order. Our framework applies broadly to crystalline systems hosting locally symmetry-lowered environments embedded within a higher-symmetry global structure. We identify how directional elastic forces organize displacement correlations and how eliminating internal coordinates generates staggered antisymmetric interactions-a phononic analogue of Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya exchange-even in globally centrosymmetric crystals. By separating intersite angular-momentum transfer from crystalline restoring torques, we show that both elastic anisotropy and the induced antisymmetric interactions together drive oppositely circulating angular-momentum currents on neighboring plaquettes, despite vanishing mean angular momentum at every site. Sustained by quantum and thermal fluctuations, this circulation preserves time-reversal and inversion symmetry and requires neither external driving nor spontaneous symmetry breaking. Our results establish lattice geometry as a microscopic source of spatially organized angular-momentum dynamics.

papers.title: LeapQuant: Efficient Linear Attention with Accurate Recurrent State Quantization
papers.abstract: Recent LLMs increasingly adopt hybrid designs that replace standard attention with linear attention, such as Gated DeltaNet (GDN) and Kimi Delta Attention (KDA). Although they compress the context into a fixed-size recurrent state and substantially reduce the cost of long-context processing, repeatedly reading and updating that state remains a major inference bottleneck. Quantization offers a natural way to reduce this cost, but can significantly degrade model quality, due to the accumulation of rounding errors and the presence of outlier rows and columns in the state. To address these challenges, we propose LeapQuant, a training-free method that achieves near-lossless performance under 8-bit recurrent-state quantization. First, to mitigate error accumulation, we propose per-window quantization, which leaps over a window of tokens and quantizes the state only once at its end. Within a window, outputs are computed from the fixed low-bit state together with high-precision buffered updates. Second, to reduce the error introduced by each quantization, LeapQuant retains the state's largest outliers as a few high-precision Compensator Tokens, which share the update path of real tokens. We then smooth the remaining residual before quantization to further reduce the error. Comprehensive experiments across the Qwen, Kimi, and GLM model families show that LeapQuant substantially reduces memory and compute costs during inference. With accuracy comparable to the FP32 baseline, it achieves average speedups of 2.05--3.70$\times$ at the kernel level and 1.47$\times$ for end-to-end inference on NVIDIA B200, RTX PRO 6000, and RTX 5090 GPUs.

papers.title: Representable but Unlearned: Encoding Rank and the Interaction-Prediction Floor
papers.abstract: Input encodings can prevent a predictor from reproducing measured interactions jointly, even when each interaction is individually representable. We compute the attainable contrast space from the encoder and contrast design, without labels or predictor fitting. Projecting measured contrasts onto this space gives an empirical squared-error floor for any deterministic decoder using the encoding. On an siRNA panel, a graph neural network's training-only feature mask merges 165 measured states into 90 classes, reducing the rank of 140 interaction contrasts to 72. The floor is 0.009980, or 14.63% of recorded contrast energy, the mean squared error of predicting zero for every contrast. Its 14.6% share of fitted interaction error adds little: predicted interactions are nearly zero, and their MSE of 0.068335 slightly exceeds that of the same control. Antisense-marginal shares are larger: 36.49% of recorded energy and 38.1% of fitted error. Three restored chemistry columns suffice for full rank. Removing the full mask eliminates the floor, but refitting improves interaction MSE by only 0.000017; the restored features remain absent from training inputs. Two further panels clarify the diagnostic's scope. A released splicing predictor encodes injectively and retains the full design rank of 1,986, so its floor is zero. For an independent count-fingerprint encoder on a lipid panel, 800 pairwise-distinct encoded contrast rows have rank 740, exposing 60 restrictions missed by duplicate-row checks. The diagnostic identifies encoding-imposed limits and can trace them to specific features. It separates representability from learned accuracy, but does not by itself predict refitting gains or explain the remaining error.

papers.title: CRF Loss is How Networks Should Learn Boundaries in Weakly Supervised Segmentation
papers.abstract: Weakly Supervised Semantic Segmentation (WSSS) learns pixel-level predictions from image-level tags. Recent work focuses on improving coarse CAMs extracted from large vision-language models (commonly CLIP), but does little to improve their accuracy along segment boundaries. That job is instead delegated to a post-processing method like DenseCRF. However, because DenseCRF relies on low-level colour cues, it can flip correct labels to incorrect ones when neighbouring pixels share similar colours. SAM has recently been adopted as a natural alternative, yet it simply takes on DenseCRF's role as an intermediate "refinement" step that outputs one-hot pseudo-labels in prior work. By discarding the valuable uncertainty in CAMs, these one-hot pseudo-labels turn borderline errors into confidently wrong targets. Our key insight is that CAMs should supervise training alongside SAM boundaries, each through its own loss, rather than being fused together into a single hard target. Inspired by CRF potentials, we propose a framework that disentangles soft pseudo-labels as unary supervision and binary edge maps as pairwise supervision. We realize our framework in a single-stage model, DS-CRF, using CAMs from dino.txt and boundaries from SAM. DS-CRF sets a new state-of-the-art of 56.5% mIoU on MS COCO among single-stage methods.

papers.title: Dynamic Service Recommendation with Congestion-Dependent Joining: Near-Optimal and Constant-Factor Approximation Algorithms
papers.abstract: Modern service platforms often show customers real-time congestion information, such as anticipated waiting times, before they decide whether to use a service. This creates an intertemporal tradeoff: directing a customer to a service may generate immediate value, but the resulting congestion can make that service less attractive to future customers. We study this tradeoff in a finite-horizon problem in which a platform recommends one of multiple services, each represented by a queue, and customers' joining probabilities decrease with congestion. We show that optimal recommendations generally depend on the joint congestion state and cannot be reduced to indices that depend only on each service's own state. Hence, exact dynamic programming suffers from a curse of dimensionality. We develop approximation algorithms that retain progressively less of this joint state. First, we construct a quasi-polynomial-time approximation scheme that achieves a $(1-ε)$-approximation for any $ε>0$. It rounds the model primitives and truncates the relevant queue lengths to compress the joint state into a histogram over service types, and our coupling arguments bound the resulting revenue loss. Second, under general monotone joining and service capacities, we study policies that retain only per-service information. A greedy policy, which uses only each service's current queue length, is a tight $1/2$-approximation, as it ignores the congestion externality that a customer imposes on later customers. An LP-guided algorithm that plans each service's queue-length distribution over the horizon accounts for this externality and achieves a $(1-1/e)$-approximation. Finally, monotone joining is what makes the problem tractable: with nonempty initial queues, both constant-factor guarantees hold under monotonicity, whereas without it the problem is NP-hard to approximate within any constant factor.

papers.title: Hull Games of Induced Path Convexities in Graphs
papers.abstract: In 1984, Frank Harary introduced the first convexity games in graphs, all of them based on the geodesic convexity, which is the graph convexity related to shortest paths. In 2024, Araújo et al. obtained the first PSPACE-hardness proofs on some of these geodesic games and generalized them to any graph convexity. In this paper, we investigate convexity games on several known induced path convexities: the monophonic $\mathrm{m}$-convexity and the $\ell_k$-convexities, based on induced paths and on induced paths of size at most $k$. We prove that the hull games $\mathrm{CHG}_{\mathrm{m}}$, $\mathrm{CHG}_{\ell_k}$ and their misère variants are PSPACE-complete for every $k\ge2$ even in graphs with diameter at most 3. We also use the Sprague-Grundy Theory to obtain a polynomial time algorithm to decide the winner of the games $\mathrm{CHG}_{\mathrm{m}}$ and $\mathrm{CHG}_{\ell_k}$ for any $k\ge2$ in disjoint unions of paths and cycles. For $k\ge3$ odd, we prove that Alice (1st player) wins $\mathrm{CHG}_{\ell_k}$ in the path $P_n$ if and only if $n$ is odd and she wins in the cycle $C_n$ if and only if $n=3$ or $n=α\cdot (k+1)-1$ with $α\ge2$. For $k\ge2$ even, the only periodic nimber sequences of $\mathrm{CHG}_{\ell_k}$ obtained through extensive computational testing occurred for $k=2^h-4$ with $h\ge3$, e.g, $k\in\{4,12,28,60,\ldots\}$. In this case ($k=2^h-4$ with $h\ge3$), we prove that the nimber sequences of $\mathrm{CHG}_{\ell_k}$ in $P_n$ and in $C_n$ are periodic and Alice loses (resp. wins) in $P_n$ (resp. $C_n$) with $n>k$ only when $n=3k+4$ (resp. $n\in\{2k+1,5k+3\}$). Finally, we show that, for $k=2$, the game $\mathrm{CHG}_{\ell_2}$ in paths $P_n$ is closely related to the classical game \emph{Couples-are-Forever} of J. H. Conway: it is still an open problem if the nimber sequence is periodic or not and Alice loses only for 12 values of $n$ up to $200$ million.

papers.title: Tachyonic particle production in strongly supercooled phase transitions
papers.abstract: In strongly supercooled cosmological phase transitions, which generically lead to strong, observable gravitational-wave backgrounds, the scalar field typically transitions to a value well below the minimum of its potential. We study particle production caused by the subsequent evolution of the field. Because some modes feature temporarily tachyonic masses, they can be efficiently produced, and a significant fraction of the energy density released in the phase transition can get converted to particles rather than gradient energy. This has consequences for the shape and amplitude of the gravitational-wave spectrum caused by the interactions in bubbles and sources a new, high-frequency signal.

papers.title: Tight Lower Bounds for Differentially Private Continual Counting
papers.abstract: The Binary Tree Mechanism is a standard algorithm for differentially private continual counting, but its complete asymptotic optimality under differential privacy has remained unresolved since its introduction. We resolve this question. For $0 \leq \varepsilon \leq 1$, we prove asymptotically tight lower bounds for $\ell_\infty$, mean squared, and maximum per-coordinate expected squared error simultaneously under all regimes of $0 \leq δ\leq 1/4$. These bounds hold for arbitrary mechanisms, even when the entire stream is available in advance. Our lower bounds match the (blocked) Binary Tree Mechanism instantiated with the best of Laplace or Gaussian noise, establishing its asymptotic optimality. Our proof uses a single hard distribution where elements are ``tagged'' as potentially being the target flipped element via a score evaluated down a tree. A simple modification of the score allows the same framework to establish tight lower bounds for all three error measures.

papers.title: BEAM3R: Beam's-eye-view architecture with Mamba-3 for implicit dose reconstruction
papers.abstract: To enable accurate and rapid photon control point and proton beamlet dose calculation in the DoseRAD2026 challenge, we present BEAM3R, a dose estimation framework operating in beam's-eye-view (BEV). Our core innovation combines a Mamba-3 state-space depth-sequence core with physics-based transport conditioning to model long-range depth transport without expensive 3D convolutions. BEAM3R shares a 2D CNN encoder-decoder architecture for photon and proton dose tasks, processing per-plane BEV slices. Proton beamlets are conditioned on water equivalent thickness and remaining range, encoding the parameters determining Bragg peak position. Photon models use a bidirectional Mamba-3 core to capture dose contributions from materials downstream of the calculation point, while the proton model uses a forward core with learned energy-prefix tokens and a Bragg-peak refinement module. To reduce interpolation artifacts and support high spatial resolution, we introduce axial grid alignment of BEV lattices with CT slices and an implicit super-resolution representation arranged as channels, evaluated by a differentiable Triton-accelerated resampler that reconstructs packed cubic B-spline coefficients directly in CT space. For MRI-based tasks, synthetic CTs (sCT) are generated using a conditional GAN with a SwinUNETR generator and a PatchGAN discriminator. On the preliminary DoseRAD2026 test set, CT-to-photon and CT-to-proton models achieved 1%/1 mm local gamma pass rates of 96.8% and 96.0%, with stratified plan-level MAEs of 0.0041 and 0.0079. Substituting sCT reduced gamma pass rates to 89.7% for photon and 75.4% proton plan level doses, with stratified plan-level MAEs of 0.0093 and 0.0336. Standardised runtimes were 23.4 s and 18.4 s for CT-to-photon and CT-to-proton prediction, increasing to 39.7 s and 42.8 s for the corresponding MRI-based pipelines.

papers.title: Enhanced Multifractality Induced by Non-Hermitian Disorder in Quantum Percolation
papers.abstract: We study the two-dimensional quantum site-percolation model with reciprocal hopping and random imaginary on-site potentials, which describe spatially uncorrelated gain and loss. The localization properties of the eigenstates are characterized through the complex spacing ratio, the participation entropy, and the generalized fractal dimensions $D_q$. Finite-size scaling yields an effective quantum percolation threshold $p_q$ that increases monotonically with $γ$, with a shift larger than that produced by a real on-site potential of equal strength. We show that the onset of extended behavior drifts toward larger occupation probabilities as the system size increases. The localization--delocalization change is therefore a crossover, consistent with the absence of a sharp transition for reciprocal non-Hermitian disorder in two dimensions. Accordingly, the interval between the classical threshold $p_c$ and $p_q$ constitutes an extended multifractal crossover regime and its width at accessible sizes grows with $γ$. Although all states are expected to localize in the thermodynamic limit, above $p_q$ the localization length exceeds the largest system size simulated, which is already larger than current photonic samples. The size-dependent threshold and the multifractal regime, which widens with the loss strength and can therefore be reached without fine-tuning, are thus directly accessible in photonic waveguide lattices.

papers.title: The Memory Trust Gap: Reliance on Stale Evidence Across Model Scales in LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Persistent-memory agents can follow stale information despite current authoritative evidence. We study stale-evidence reliance across Qwen3 0.6/1.7/4/8B checkpoints using two controlled, action-scored suites: a Benefit suite requiring stored information and a Safety suite providing current evidence as static prompt text. We distinguish stale-value reliance from net accuracy loss relative to no memory. Benefit-suite reliance is 0.92-1.00 across checkpoints. In the Safety suite, larger checkpoints resist a plain stale note but incur substantial harm when it appears newer. A full $2\times2\times2\times2$ factorial manipulates label, recency, source authority, and position. Direct cross-size contrasts identify stronger recency effects in the larger tested checkpoints and a position-effect sign reversal within Qwen3. Metadata improves accuracy at all four checkpoints, with larger gains at 4B/8B; pre-resolution yields near-ceiling accuracy across all four. Llama-Instruct comparisons provide cross-family evidence for selected effects, while RGB and MisBench corroborate stale-value reliance. A framing control shows that the failure extends beyond memory-labeled content. These results characterize cue-dependent vulnerability across tested checkpoints without isolating capability or evaluating a complete memory lifecycle.

papers.title: Optimal Uniform Pricing for Multi-Interval Dispatch without Make-Whole Uplifts
papers.abstract: In a network with ramp-limited generators and inaccurate net-demand forecasts, practical rolling-window dispatch can drive locational marginal prices (LMPs) below generators' bid-in offers. In such cases, out-of-market (OOM) settlements are used to compensate generators and maintain dispatch-following incentives, but OOM can have negative consequences, including nontransparent real-time price signals, discriminatory compensation, and incentives for untruthful bidding. This paper presents an optimal uniform pricing rule that minimizes demand payments, eliminates OOM make-whole payments, preserves LMP-based congestion charges, and ensures revenue adequacy. We derive the proposed pricing rule in closed form and relate it to existing pricing schemes. Numerical comparisons demonstrate favorable generator profits and reduced price volatility. However, higher generator profits are accompanied by increased demand payments, reflecting the in-market, uniform allocation of ramping costs while preserving the LMP-based congestion charges widely used in real-time market settlements. The numerical results also show that, under LMP with OOM settlement, a price-taking generator has an incentive to inflate its offer, whereas this incentive is absent under the proposed pricing rule within the tested bid range.

papers.title: Mixture of Polyconvex Neural Potentials for Parametric Hyperelasticity: Towards Foundation Material Models
papers.abstract: Hyperelastic constitutive models enable modeling large deformations in elastic solids. In common practice, a strain energy density function is prescribed in advance and model-specific parameters are calibrated from experiments. However, many applications require constitutive models for a family of related materials whose mechanical behavior varies with composition. A fixed constitutive model-form may not capture the full range of behavior across the family, while fitting separate forms does not provide a direct way to predict the response of new compositions. Recent work has developed data-driven constitutive models that learn flexible strain energy functions while incorporating key physical constraints. In this work, we propose using mixtures of convex neural potentials based on input convex neural networks as a modular and data efficient approach to modeling material families. Each potential is convex and monotonic with respect to polyconvex strain invariants, while a conditioning network maps material descriptors to mixture weights. We compare the approach with a monolithic partially input-convex neural network using experimental data from PolyJet 3D-printed materials and a synthetic Gent-type benchmark. Across both benchmarks, the mixture architecture generalized better to material descriptors not seen during training. In the PolyJet experimental benchmark, we showed that the mixture architecture is less sensitive to model hyperparameters, while in the Gent-type benchmark it generalized more reliably with sparse data in the material-descriptor space. These results suggest that representing a material family through a small set of shared convex neural potentials provides a useful structural prior for learning descriptor-dependent constitutive behavior from limited data.

papers.title: Band edges of periodic Schrödinger operators are generically isolated and nondegenerate
papers.abstract: For periodic Schrödinger operators $H_V=-Δ+V$ with bounded real-valued potentials on $\mathbb R^d$ with $d\ge2$, we show that for generic potentials, each endpoint of every spectral gap is attained by a single Bloch band at only finitely many quasimomenta, and has a nondegenerate Hessian at every attaining point. This proves the Spectral Edge Conjecture for periodic Schrödinger operators.

papers.title: Tropical Matsusaka and Matsusaka--Ran Criteria
papers.abstract: The tropical Schottky problem asks which principally polarized tropical abelian varieties are isomorphic to tropical Jacobian varieties equipped with their canonical principal polarizations. We prove the tropical Matsusaka criterion and the tropical Matsusaka--Ran criterion, which are the main results of this paper, and show that their hypotheses are equivalent. Together with the tropical Poincaré formula proved by Gross--Shokrieh, these results give a geometric solution to the tropical Schottky problem. In particular, we give an affirmative answer to a question posed by Brannetti--Melo--Viviani. Several tools are developed for the proofs of the two criteria. In particular, we establish Hodge-type inequalities for ample tropical Cartier divisors on tropical abelian varieties and prove a splitting criterion for principally polarized tropical abelian varieties.

papers.title: Fair Division Under Boolean Valuations: Beyond Normalization
papers.abstract: We study fair division of indivisible items when agents have arbitrary two-level preferences: the value of each agent for any set of items is Boolean, which need not be monotone or additive. Notably, we do not impose the standard assumption of normalization, i.e., different agents may value the empty set at different Boolean levels. Since the preferences are nonmonotone, envy-freeness up to one item (EF1) and envy-freeness up to any item (EFX) each admit several variants, depending on which items are tested for removal and whether they are removed from the envious agent's bundle or the envied agent's bundle. This paper investigates the existence of these variants of EF1 and EFX, on their own and together with economic efficiency, incentive compatibility, feasibility constraints, and lottery-based randomization. Our paper presents a wide range of positive and negative results that collectively highlight an interesting phenomenon: the landscape of achievable guarantees depends crucially on the number of normalized agents, who value the empty bundle at the lower Boolean level.

papers.title: Representation Learning with Quantum Signal Processing
papers.abstract: Representation learning begins when training changes the features that define similarity between data. A frozen-kernel model only reweights a fixed geometry. We establish quantum signal processing (QSP) as a solvable quantum model of the representation-learning regime. At arbitrary depth, we compute the exact mean and variance of its quantum neural tangent kernel, revealing an input-dependent angular geometry whose diagonal remains non-self-averaging even when the underlying unitary approaches Haar randomness. We also prove a sparse-data guarantee for the full nonlinear gradient flow without freezing or ensemble-averaging the kernel: the realized dynamics converges to an integrable scalar flow with a time-dependent kernel closure and explicit convergence times. A finite-depth speed limit holds for every data set and trajectory. At higher data density, numerical results show coupled evolution beyond both the scalar and frozen-kernel descriptions. These results give a controlled theory of learned quantum data geometry with provable training dynamics beyond the frozen limit.

papers.title: A Unified Tracer Analysis of DESI DR2 Baryon Acoustic Oscillations
papers.abstract: We improve upon previous efforts to optimally combine overlapping galaxy samples in the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) analysis. By weighting each galaxy by its linear bias, overlapping galaxies are combined into a single, unified catalog, naturally avoiding double counting of cosmic volume and including all auto- and cross- information at the catalog level. Improvements over the previous effort include the addition of quasars out to $z=1.6$ to account for all overlapping DR2 tracers and redshift-dependent bias treatment to improve reconstruction. We report distance measurements using this unified tracer, and find them to be highly consistent with the baseline DR2 BAO analysis. We also test for tracer-dependent systematics within the DESI data, and find no evidence of tracer-dependent systematics within $0.8<z<1.6$. Finally, we take advantage of the unified tracer to rebin the analysis in redshift in order to more finely resolve the redshift-to-distance relation. Dynamical dark energy results on this finer redshift binning indicate that there is no missed feature in the expansion history in the redshifts $0.8<z<1.6$, and reproduces DESI's preference for an evolving dark energy equation of state.

papers.title: Towards Efficient Auto-Interpretability of Boltz-1 Sparse Autoencoders
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) could turn AI models in Biology and other fields into engines of scientific discovery by explaining the superhuman capabilities of those models. We postulate that a latent is useful if we know three things: whether it is coherent, whether it can be described, and whether that description has predictive power. These questions are routinely conflated. We assemble them into a single pipeline and report some practical innovations. First, cross-seed dictionary stability prioritises which latents are worth spending resources to investigate. Second, an intruder-detection task asks whether a latent's activating examples share a recognizable pattern. Third, a separate pass proposes a candidate biological description which we convert into falsifiable predictions which can be tested in silico. Deployed on the Boltz-1 Pairformer trunk, stability prioritisation finds interpretable latents using about 4.4 times fewer latent evaluations each, and at 5.2 times lower measured LLM cost, while recovering over half of them. However, we notice that in our setup the LLM judge is heavily biased towards consistent residue identity and a simple filter that selects for features with high amino-acid identity precision outperforms the stability thresholding. This simpler method has the added benefit of requiring no extra SAE seeds but it remains uncertain if it reflects a genuinely useful heuristic or an limitation of the LLM judge.

papers.title: IoMT-SecAlarmBench: A Semi-Synthetic Counterfactual Benchmark for Integrity Attacks in IoMT
papers.abstract: The Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) combines clinical physiological data with cyber-system information, creating challenges in determining whether an abnormal reading reflects a genuine physiological event, a device fault, or a cyber-attack within the expected physiological range. Answering this requires counterfactual ground truth, which no existing dataset provides. We present IoMT-SecAlarmBench, a semi-synthetic benchmark that injects controlled integrity attacks into genuine coupled ECG+PPG recordings using a structured experimental design combining four attack morphologies, four severity levels, two physiological plausibility conditions, and replay attacks. Each injected window retains its cause, attack subtype, and the clean signal that would have been observed without the attack. We evaluate six detectors from five method families using threshold-independent measures and a matched false-alarm budget. Results show no method consistently detects the most difficult cases: replay attacks and low-amplitude transient spikes remain close to chance-level performance across detectors. Results also reveal a trade-off between detecting attacks and distinguishing them from sensor faults: the best-performing detector on hard cases flags fault/artifact windows at 5.3 times its false-alarm rate on normal data. Three-way classification performs poorly for genuine physiological events, and a leakage audit of a dual-modality network dataset indicates previously reported IoMT intrusion-detection performance is partly driven by identifying information. Benchmark, generation code, preprocessing, evaluation tools, and datasheet are released.

papers.title: Probing and steering biology across Boltz-1s trunk-diffusion boundary
papers.abstract: AlphaFold3-class structure predictors pair a representational trunk, which processes sequence and context, with a diffusion module, which generates atomic coordinates. How biological information changes as it crosses this architectural boundary remains poorly understood. We analyze per-residue activations from the Pairformer trunk and diffusion module of Boltz-1 using linear probes, sparse autoencoders (SAEs), and causal interventions. From the trunk, both geometry (secondary structure, disorder) and sequence chemistry (amino-acid identity, signal peptides, disulfide-bond annotations) are linearly decodable. In the diffusion module, the two diverge. Secondary structure remains equally decodable, whereas sequence chemistry becomes much less linearly accessible. We then test whether decodable directions can steer the model by editing the trunk's single representation. Helix and coil directions change predicted structure dose-dependently, but a beta-strand direction that is highly predictive on the same proteins (held-out F1 =0.78) produces no measurable increase in strand content at any of the steered layers. Removing helix or coil directions does not remove that structure. Linear decodability therefore did not imply causal influence at the sites we tested. The same probes also score markedly lower against SwissProt annotations than against DSSP labels, because unannotated residues that the model gets right are charged as false positives; such scores are therefore lower bounds. Finally, supervised probes outscore single SAE features wherever a label already exists.

papers.title: Critical avalanche tails in the one-dimensional anisotropic Bak--Sneppen model
papers.abstract: We study avalanche ranges in the anisotropic Bak-Sneppen model on $\mathbb Z$. In exponential coordinates, the right endpoint $X_t$ of an avalanche started at the origin has a nonlinear jump evolution whose tails satisfy a closed triangular system. Write $m(t)=\mathbb E[X_t]$ and let $t_c$ be the threshold for finite $m(t)$. Below $t_c$, the endpoint has exponential moments and $m(t)\sim 2/(t_c-t)$. At criticality it is finite almost surely, but $\mathbb P(X_{t_c}\geq k)\geq ck^{-1/2}$ and $\mathbb E[X_{t_c}^{1/3}]=\infty$. We propose two approaches for the critical estimates. First, a simple compensation argument, based on an extremal inequality for decreasing probability masses, yields a $k^{-2/3}$ lower bound. This already proves equality of the susceptibility and infinite-avalanche thresholds. We then exploit the additional fact that the exact evolution preserves geometric mixtures for the tails, which sharpens the bound to $k^{-1/2}$. Finally, by freezing the grafting law at criticality, we prove that the avalanche is infinite with positive probability for every $t>t_c$.

papers.title: The Nuclear Decision-Making Benchmark: Evaluating Frontier LLM Tendencies in Escalation, Proliferation, Non-Proliferation, and Arms Control Scenarios
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are entering defense and national-security workflows. Seven of the nine nuclear-armed states have committed to keeping humans in control of decisions to use nuclear weapons, but LLMs may still shape the assessments and options that reach decision-makers. Scrutinizing that influence calls for evidence about how these models behave on nuclear-policy questions. Such evidence should cover more than crisis escalation and should separate a model's tendencies from artifacts of a single phrasing, ordering, or run; evaluations to date have not focused on these questions. We introduce the Nuclear Decision-Making Benchmark (NDM Bench), a dataset and reproducible framework for testing how the choice of model and the design of a question shape LLMs' answers on nuclear policy. Its 151 scenarios, written by international relations experts, span four domains: nuclear escalation (76), arms control (25), non-proliferation (25), and proliferation (25). Each scenario can be posed with different states in the decision-maker's role and with added framing sentences. Eight frontier LLMs answered every prompt five times, about 380{,}000 responses in all. Results highlight that models' choices differ by model and domain, and that in escalation, how often they choose a nuclear threat or nuclear use depends on the state being advised and, for some models, the framing. However, agreement across identical runs is often low, with all five runs agreeing on only 43\% of escalation prompts. We release the scenarios, the prompts with their answer orders, and the parsed responses, along with documentation of how they were built and recommended practices for evaluations where there is no correct answer to grade against.

papers.title: Gravitational Memory Beyond Null Infinity through Finite-Distance Carrollian Screens
papers.abstract: We investigate gravitational memory beyond null infinity by studying finite-distance null hypersurfaces endowed with Carrollian geometry. We show that the intrinsic degenerate geometry, optical data, and null Brown--York tensor of a finite null screen define a quasilocal Carrollian dissipative system, providing a natural framework to characterize the residual geometric response after the passage of radiation. To make this construction explicit and compare it with the standard asymptotic description, we use Robinson--Trautman spacetimes as an exactly solvable radiative setting. For asymptotically flat Robinson--Trautman geometries, we transform the solution to Bondi gauge and extract the asymptotic data directly in terms of the Robinson--Trautman field. In the linearized sector, the Bondi shear is purely electric and produces the standard displacement-memory effect associated with the relaxation toward the final Schwarzschild geometry. We show that the leading large-radius tracefree component of the finite-screen memory reduces to the Bondi displacement memory, while finite-distance corrections retain additional focusing, embedding dependence, angular drift, Coulombic data, and near-zone information. Thus, Bondi memory emerges as the universal asymptotic projection of a broader quasilocal Carrollian response. Late-time screens approaching the final Schwarzschild horizon exhibit exponentially decaying non-isotropic Carrollian data, leaving only the isotropic null Brown--York stress. As a by-product, we construct the Robinson--Trautman solution with nonzero cosmological constant to second order in the radiative amplitude and use the holographic dictionary to study the associated energy fluxes and find that the resulting charge does not obey a universal monotonicity property.

papers.title: The muon Moonshot: Moon subsurface tomography with upward-going muons
papers.abstract: We propose a novel muon Moonshot concept for lunar subsurface tomography based on upward-going muons originating from the lunar regolith. Unlike Earth, the Moon lacks an atmosphere, leaving dense regolith below and a near-vacuum environment above. Consequently, most downward-going hadrons are absorbed before decaying, while upward-going hadrons escaping the regolith can decay in flight, producing a significant flux of lunar muons. These muons can be detected by instruments on the lunar surface or in near-lunar orbit. We perform Monte Carlo simulations to investigate their energy spectra, angular distributions, and integrated fluxes under various theoretical and detector configurations. The results indicate that the lunar muon flux is sensitive to detector altitude under idealized geometry. This dependence demonstrates its potential as a novel, non-invasive probe of shallow subsurface voids. We also present case studies on the detection of underground cavities and water resources. For shallow overburden, large cavity signals remain detectable with estimated backgrounds and systematics. Weaker water signals remain challenging. Potential implementations in future lunar missions are also discussed.

papers.title: Large-Load Demand Flexibility as Virtual Storage
papers.abstract: Water electrolysis plants, hyperscale data centers, and aluminum potlines represent gigawatts of demand-side flexibility for bulk power system balancing, operational planning, and procurement services. Such loads are scheduled through per-interval power bounds and horizon energy windows, whereas co-located battery energy storage systems (BESS) operate under state-of-charge dynamics. The two formulations share no common mathematical structure, and the joint procurement value of co-located loads and storage goes unrealized as a result. This paper establishes the connection between the two formulations through a virtual storage (VS) equivalence. Every feasible large-load trajectory under power-bound and energy-window constraints is a valid charge trajectory of a VS device that operates at unity accounting efficiency in the grid power balance. Production and service-level costs lie outside this abstraction and enter the dispatch through curtailment opportunity costs. For a portfolio co-located with a BESS, aggregation reduces the constraint count from O(NT) to O(T) and yields a co-dispatch price for both resources. Validation on the IEEE RTS-GMLC with three representative load classes shows that virtual storage delivers the dominant share of joint procurement savings. In the tested case, savings are additive because the two resources dispatch to non-overlapping intervals, and the curtailment shadow price tracks the peak-price band onset rather than the daily peak price.

papers.title: The Language-Energy Divide: Measuring Energy Costs of Multilingual LLM Inference
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in multilingual settings, yet the energy costs of serving these models across different languages remain poorly understood. We present a systematic study of inference energy consumption across languages with ML.Energy framework (Chung et al., 2026). We find striking disparities: energy consumption per output token varies by up to 8.3 times across languages, while total energy for a fixed set of requests varies by up to 179 times between the cheapest (English, 17.6 kJ) and the most expensive (Pashto, 3,147 kJ) languages. Our analysis shows that this disparity is driven by two compounding factors: (1) higher per-token energy costs for languages using complex or rare scripts, and (2) more tokens generated for low-resource languages. Moreover, we find a double cost + performance penalty: languages with the highest energy footprints also tend to achieve the lowest task accuracy. We reveal that the energy divide persists across models, hardware, and tasks, suggesting a systemic energy inequity in multilingual LLM deployment. Finally, we recommend that the community treat energy as a first-class evaluation axis, extend reporting checklists and model cards to include it, and adopt deployment-side mitigations for better energy efficiency.

papers.title: Multi-Stage Stochastic Optimization and Reinforcement Learning Approaches for Dynamic Inspection of Infrastructure Systems
papers.abstract: We study a dynamic inspection problem for infrastructure systems in which we route and schedule multiple vehicles to monitor components that are subject to heterogeneous stochastic failures. Inspection decisions determine which components the vehicles serve first and thus affect how failures propagate to neighboring components. We formulate the problem as a multi-stage stochastic mixed-integer program that jointly optimizes routing and scheduling under exogenous and decision-dependent uncertainty. We develop a stochastic dual dynamic integer programming (SDDiP) algorithm based on a stage decomposition of the multi-stage model and show that it converges finitely to the optimal value. In parallel, we propose a reinforcement learning (RL) approach that learns assignment policies from simulated system dynamics. On instances built from the road and storm-sewer networks of Sioux Falls, SDDiP proves optimality where the extended formulation of the same model leaves large gaps. On larger instances, RL with a routable-assignment certificate often finds cheaper policies than SDDiP under a short computational budget, whereas SDDiP finds cheaper policies and bounds on their quality with more time. Moreover, modeling failure propagation and decision-dependent transition probabilities reduces the realized cost when these mechanisms are present. These comparisons guide the choice between optimization and policy learning for inspection planning under failure risk.

papers.title: Weyl conformal geometry vs Riemannian geometry of Weyl gauge invariant (dressed) metric
papers.abstract: Weyl conformal geometry is the natural underlying geometry of gauge theories of Weyl group (of dilatations and Poincaré symmetry), such as Weyl quadratic gravity and its generalisation, Weyl-Dirac-Born-Infeld action (WDBI). These are local, Weyl-anomaly free (quantum) gauge theories of gravity. We describe Weyl gauge symmetry from a more familiar Riemannian view of Weyl gauge invariant dressed fields by the Wilson line of dilatations. Weyl geometry can then be seen as Riemannian geometry of non-local dressed metric ($g_{μν}^*$), at the "cost" of (gauge-induced) non-commutativity in the UV, due to Wilson line. Then Weyl quadratic gravity and WDBI actions of Weyl geometry, which are Weyl gauge invariant in $d$ dimensions, have the same expression in Riemannian geometry defined by $g^*_{μν}$. This is a non-local map and dual description of the two geometries and actions in the symmetric phase. Unlike for the metric, the equation of motion of Weyl gauge field ($ω_μ$) does not commute with the dressing of the metric. Quantum non-locality, in particular entanglement, and non-commutativity are (gauge-invariant) physical artefacts of "translating" (local) Weyl geometry and Weyl gauge covariance into our real-world Riemannian geometry of Weyl gauge invariant observables, and they are evidence of Weyl gauge symmetry. At lower energies, $ω_μ$ becomes massive, can decouple and Einstein-Hilbert action and commutativity are recovered. The case of a light $ω_μ$ is also discussed.

papers.title: A counterexample to a basis conjecture of Brualdi, Friedland, and Pothen
papers.abstract: Brualdi, Friedland, and Pothen conjectured that certain rank inequalities characterize bases consisting of elementary vectors in the row space of a matrix whose nonzero entries are algebraically independent. We give a $4\times6$ counterexample: all the inequalities hold, but the four elementary vectors form a minimally dependent family. A construction using two planes in a common three-dimensional subspace explains the dependence and gives a second counterexample pattern with only four prescribed zeros. We also prove that the proposed criterion is valid over every field when the number of columns exceeds the row rank by at most one. A direct-sum extension gives counterexamples of size $m\times(m+2)$ for every $m\ge4$. Thus the minimum column excess permitting a counterexample is exactly two in every such rank.

papers.title: Tax Salience: How Requiring Transparency Affects the Price of Equality
papers.abstract: Less-salient taxes can ease the classic trade-off between equality and efficiency by making people respond less to taxation. But deliberately obscuring taxes may be viewed as dishonest. This creates a three-way trade-off between equality, efficiency, and honesty. We analyze this trade-off in a simple setting with a linear income tax. We define and characterize the morally efficient frontier, trading off utilitarian welfare against honesty or transparency. Complete honesty is Pareto inefficient but not morally inefficient. More generally, increasing honesty reduces utilitarian welfare. When utilitarian welfare is decomposed into equality and efficiency, the cost of honesty falls most robustly on equality: Higher salience always reduces equality, while the effect on efficiency is ambiguous. This asymmetry arises because salience increases the price of equality, which is the efficiency cost of a marginal increase in equality. Our approach could be applied to other settings in which utilitarian and procedural or deontological values conflict.

papers.title: Latent Q-Barrier Shielding for Safe In-Context Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Safe in-context reinforcement learning (ICRL) adapts online from interaction history without test-time parameter updates while controlling episode cost under a safety budget. Under out-of-distribution (OOD) deployment shifts, pretraining-only safe ICRL can give poor reward-safety tradeoffs because the remaining budget affects behavior only through frozen policy conditioning, not an explicit action-level check against predicted future cost. We propose a latent Q-Barrier shield that learns a context representation, latent dynamics, and an ensemble cost critic before deployment. Without parameter updates, the shield infers context from history and filters or softly reweights candidate actions using the remaining budget and predicted future cost. We prove a conditional one-step barrier-margin bound over realized candidate sets, with explicit Bellman and latent-prediction error terms. Across five safe ICRL benchmarks, the shield improves deployment-time reward-safety tradeoffs over a strong safe-ICRL baseline: after a short context window, it achieves higher return in four of five benchmarks while matching or lowering average episode cost in all five. Code is available at https://github.com/kmj1122/q-barrier.

papers.title: Step in Tine: Forking Processes in Functional Choreographies
papers.abstract: Choreographic programming allows a concurrent programmer to write one centralized program and compile it to individual programs for each system participant. This approach simplifies critical properties like deadlock freedom, but it complicates forking new processes, a core concurrent primitive. This work addresses that gap with the choreographic fork calculus $λ{\pitchfork}$, the first functional choreographic language with process spawning. $λ{\pitchfork}$ provides a deadlock-freedom guarantee while allowing programs to dynamically determine when to spawn new processes, what they will do, and who will communicate with them. All results are formalized in Lean.

papers.title: HolisticMotion: Holistic Modeling for Motion Reconstruction from Sparse Tracking
papers.abstract: Reconstructing full-body motion from sparse tracking signals is crucial for immersive AR/VR applications. Existing methods predominantly adopt a sensor-centric observation perspective, learning full-body representations primarily under sparse conditioning, while additional joint observations available during training remain underutilized as inputs. We propose HolisticMotion, which shifts the modeling perspective toward holistic full-body modeling by treating every joint as a potential input source within a unified skeletal layout. Guided by this holistic perspective, we introduce three complementary designs. First, a curriculum masking strategy bridges full-body motion learning and sparse inference by gradually shifting training from a mixture of masked full-body and sparse inputs to exclusively sparse inputs. Second, body partitioning models region dynamics and helps preserve local motion cues. Third, Kinematic Attention coordinates body regions by combining dynamic spatial interactions with learnable structural priors inspired by the kinematic tree. Experiments on AMASS and HPS demonstrate competitive reconstruction performance across various tracking protocols, with the lowest positional errors among the compared methods. The unified representation also accommodates additional wearable sensors, yielding further improvements in reconstruction accuracy and motion smoothness.

papers.title: Contractibility of the Gromov--Hausdorff cloud of a Hilbert space
papers.abstract: The cloud of a metric space $X$ consists of all metric spaces at finite Gromov--Hausdorff distance from $X$, with spaces at zero distance identified. We prove that the cloud of every real Hilbert space $H$ admits a strong deformation retraction onto the point represented by $H$.

papers.title: Unexpected Marangoni Condensation in Negative Binary Mixtures
papers.abstract: Marangoni condensation - where surface tension gradients induce instabilities that lead to condensate film breakup into discrete droplets - has traditionally been considered limited to positive binary mixtures, where the less volatile component has higher surface tension. Negative mixtures were expected to exhibit stable filmwise condensation. Here, we demonstrate unexpected spontaneous Marangoni-driven pseudo-dropwise condensation in negative water-ethylene glycol and water-triethylene glycol mixtures. Strong thermo-diffusion in these dilute mixtures enables preferential glycol enrichment in colder condensate film regions during condensation, generating surface tension gradients that trigger film breakup, leading to greater than 6x wettability-independent heat transfer enhancement compared to filmwise condensation at moderate subcooling. Our work challenges the conventional framework that restricts Marangoni condensation to positive mixtures; a superficial classification that oversimplifies the underlying interfacial mechanisms that can trigger robust Marangoni condensation, offering new pathways for enhancing phase change heat transfer in industrial applications without the need for expensive and degradation-prone surface coatings.

papers.title: From Schrodinger Bridge to Optimal Transport over Sub-Riemannian Manifolds
papers.abstract: We study the least-energy way to reshape a probability distribution when motion is constrained to a horizontal subbundle, i.e., optimal transport and distribution steering in sub-Riemannian geometry. It is well-known that the deterministic sub-Riemannian optimal transport problem can be complicated by the non-smooth geometry. To obtain a smooth and numerically tractable formulation, we introduce small noise that aligns with the geometry and study the associated Schrödinger bridge problem. We discuss the case where the given marginals can have compact support or have sub-Gaussian tails. Under bracket-generating hypotheses, we obtain smooth, strictly positive transition densities and a forward--backward characterization of the optimal bridge, which acts as a convex selection principle among potentially many deterministic optima. This leads to a practical Sinkhorn-type algorithm with geometric constraints and we discuss it convergence in both regimes. We show that as the noise level vanishes, the unique Schrödinger bridge minimizers converge to a minimizer of the deterministic sub-Riemannian optimal transport problem. In the case of full support regime, our result illustrates that, the existence and characterization of the unique Schrödinger bridge, Sinkhorn convergence and the convex selection principle is possible only after quantifying the smoothness and positivity of the transition density. We demonstrate with a benchmark Heisenberg group.

papers.title: iMuon: Intrinsic Spectral Optimization on Riemannian Matrix Manifolds
papers.abstract: Muon and related norm-constrained optimizers, now central to large-scale learning, compute updates via a linear maximization oracle (LMO) over a matrix-norm ball in Euclidean space. However, they do not generalize cleanly to manifold-valued parameters such as low-rank factorizations, orthogonality constraints, or symmetric positive-definite (SPD) matrices. Naively restricting the Muon LMO to the tangent space (i) breaks quotient symmetries and (ii) couples the tangent-space constraint with an ambient norm bound, which obstructs closed-form solutions. We resolve both issues with a key observation: every Riemannian metric canonically lifts a unitarily invariant Euclidean norm to an intrinsic norm on each tangent space. The resulting intrinsic LMO is symmetry preserving and, under a structural condition on the scaled tangent space, reduces to a standard Euclidean LMO. Building on this, we introduce intrinsic Muon (iMuon), a unified framework with closed-form updates on the fixed-rank, SPD, Stiefel, and Grassmann manifolds for various unitarily invariant norms, including the spectral, Frobenius, and nuclear norms. We establish deterministic and stochastic convergence rates of iMuon with constants that depend only on the manifold dimension. Notably, on the fixed-rank manifold, the constant depends only on the rank, which makes the rate independent of factor conditioning and removes the runtime factor rescaling required by prior work. Experiments on LoRA fine-tuning of LLMs, image classification, and subspace learning illustrate the efficacy of the proposed approach.

papers.title: On a PDE-based material parameter identification problem with contact constraints
papers.abstract: We consider the identification of a scalar coefficient in a PDE-based parameter estimation problem with contact constraints. The considered problem can be used as an idealized model of a membrane under forces, constrained by a barrier or indenter. More generally, it serves as a benchmark for the analysis of more complex contact problems and the development of corresponding reconstruction algorithms. In this paper, we discuss both the forward and inverse parameter estimation problems, as well as uniqueness and non-uniqueness issues caused by the contact constraints. Furthermore, we consider the design and implementation of reconstruction approaches which we test on numerical examples, illustrating both uniqueness and non-uniqueness as well as parameter identifyability.

papers.title: A Line-search-free Method for Adaptive Decentralized Optimization
papers.abstract: We study decentralized optimization over networks where agents cooperatively minimize a smooth (strongly) convex sum of local losses while communicating only with immediate neighbors. Prevailing decentralized methods require either centralized knowledge of global problem and network parameters for stepsize tuning--hence impractical, or costly per-iteration line-searches that demand access to local function values. We propose line-search-free, fully decentralized algorithms in which each agent adapts its stepsize using only past local iterates and gradients--with no extra function evaluations and no global tuning. The key technical ingredient is a new Lyapunov function, from which a natural adaptive stepsize rule emerges: at each iteration, each agent selects the largest stepsize that guarantees descent, based solely on a local curvature estimate built from successive gradients. The proposed algorithms enjoy strong theoretical guarantees: sublinear convergence rates for merely convex objectives and linear rates under strong convexity.
